finding: Theory of cerebellar cortex as a learning machine: granule cells recode mossy-fiber input into a sparse expanded code, and climbing fibers instruct changes at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses (Marr predicted potentiation).
Models the cerebellum as an adaptive pattern classifier in which climbing-fiber signals weaken co-active parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses, predicting LTD a decade before it was demonstrated.
First demonstration of LTD: conjunctive stimulation of parallel fibers and climbing fibers causes long-lasting depression of parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission (rabbit flocculus).

Lesions of the ipsilateral dentate–interpositus nuclei, but not of cerebellar cortex, abolished the learned eyelid response in rabbits; nuclear neurons showed learning-related activity, and stimulating them evoked the eyelid response.
Proposes that the phylogenetically newest parts of the lateral hemispheres and dentate nucleus, expanded in humans together with frontal cortex, contribute to mental and language skills.
Patients with cerebellar lesions are impaired both in producing timed taps and in perceiving durations, suggesting a general timing function rather than a purely motor one.
Zebrin II (later identified as aldolase C) is expressed by subsets of Purkinje cells in parasagittal stripes, revealing molecular compartments conserved from fish to rat.
Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 is caused by an unstable expanded CAG (polyglutamine) repeat in the SCA1 (ATXN1) gene; longer repeats are associated with earlier onset.

mGluR1-knockout mice are ataxic and lack parallel fiber–Purkinje LTD, although PF and CF transmission appear functional, and their eyeblink conditioning is impaired. The authors attribute both the ataxia and the conditioning deficit primarily to the loss of LTD.

Retrograde transneuronal virus tracing from prefrontal area 46 labels neurons in restricted parts of the dentate nucleus (and internal pallidum), distinct from those projecting to motor cortex: anatomical substrate for cerebellar roles in cognition.
Patients with focal olivocerebellar lesions fail to adapt their throwing to prism-shifted vision, showing that the inferior olive and cerebellum are needed for this visuomotor adaptation.

Review comparing eyeblink conditioning with VOR adaptation: plasticity is distributed between cerebellar cortex and deep nuclei, the cortex is especially important for learning movement timing, and it guides learning in the nuclei.
Math1 (Atoh1)-null mice fail to form cerebellar granule neurons: the transcription factor is essential for granule-cell genesis from the rhombic lip.
SCA6 is caused by small polyglutamine (CAG) expansions in CACNA1A, the α1A subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel that is abundant in Purkinje cells.

'Cognitive dysmetria': schizophrenia as a disruption of coordination within a cortico–thalamo–cerebellar circuit, generalizing the cerebellum's role in smoothing movement to the coordination of thought.

Defines the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome: executive dysfunction, impaired spatial cognition, linguistic deficits and personality/affect change, especially after posterior-lobe and vermis lesions.
Proposes that the cerebellum learns internal models: forward models predicting the sensory consequences of commands and inverse models producing commands, possibly organized as paired modules.

Review of inferior olive microcircuitry: in glomeruli, gap-junction-coupled spines each receive an inhibitory terminal from the hindbrain and an excitatory terminal. Proposes that the olive serves both motor learning and motor timing but does not directly compare intended with achieved movements.
Sonic hedgehog from Purkinje cells drives proliferation of granule-cell precursors; blocking Shh in vivo reduces this proliferation, a pathway later tied to medulloblastoma.
Expression of cerebellar LTD requires postsynaptic clathrin-mediated endocytosis of AMPA receptors; blocking endocytosis prevents LTD.
fMRI of movements of different body parts reveals somatotopy in the human cerebellum: an inverted body map in the anterior lobe and a second map in the posterior lobe (lobule VIII).
Review: beyond parallel-fiber LTD, the cerebellum expresses many forms of synaptic and non-synaptic (intrinsic) plasticity at multiple sites in cortex and nuclei.
Developing Purkinje cells are innervated by multiple climbing fibers; one becomes functionally dominant before the weaker inputs are eliminated, establishing one-to-one innervation.
Transneuronal virus tracing in monkeys shows closed loops: the arm area of M1 exchanges input and output with lobules IV–VI, and prefrontal area 46 with Crus II.

Parallel fiber synapses show bidirectional plasticity under climbing-fiber control: PF stimulation alone induces LTP, PF plus CF induces LTD, with a higher Ca²⁺ threshold for LTD — an inverse of the hippocampal BCM rule.
Review proposing that the cerebellum is organized into discrete microcomplexes, each receiving a specific motor error signal from spinal reflex circuits via climbing fibers.
Retrograde transneuronal rabies tracing from the putamen labels dentate nucleus neurons: the cerebellum projects disynaptically, via thalamus, to the basal ganglia.

Ptf1a marks cerebellar ventricular-zone progenitors that generate GABAergic neurons. In the Ptf1a-deficient mutant cerebelless, GABAergic neurons are not produced and the cerebellar cortex is lost; Ptf1a misexpressed in glutamatergic precursors produces GABAergic neurons.
Purkinje-cell deletion of Fmr1 enhances parallel-fiber LTD, elongates spines and impairs eyeblink conditioning; fragile X patients show comparable conditioning deficits.
PLCβ3 is expressed in zebrin II-positive and PLCβ4 in zebrin II-negative Purkinje cells, forming complementary parasagittal stripes.

Preterm infants with isolated cerebellar hemorrhagic injury screened positive for autism in 37% (vs. 0% of controls) and had severe motor (48%), expressive-language (42%) and cognitive (40%) deficits; outcomes were worse with vermis injury.
Proposes that cerebellar internal models learned for movement also copy mental models held in cerebral cortex, allowing thought to be manipulated quickly and implicitly.

During smooth-pursuit learning, a complex spike on one trial is followed by depression of the same Purkinje cell's simple-spike response on the next trial: a trial-by-trial link from climbing fibers to plasticity and learning.

Neuroimaging meta-analysis: sensorimotor activity in lobules V/VI and VIII; language and verbal working memory in right VI/Crus I; spatial in left VI; executive in VI, Crus I and VIIB; emotion in VI, Crus I and vermal VII.

Review: cerebellar output targets nonmotor prefrontal and posterior parietal areas as well as motor areas, through distinct output channels of the nuclei that form closed loops with their cortical targets.
Proposes that the many descriptions of cerebellar compartments (transverse zones and stripes, longitudinal zones and microzones, patches) chart a single underlying map.
The adult male human brain contains on average about 86 billion neurons and a similar number of non-neuronal cells; only 19% of the neurons are in the cerebral cortex.
Crus I and Crus II, the lobules linked with prefrontal cortex, occupy a significantly larger fraction of cerebellar volume in humans than in chimpanzees and capuchins.
The subthalamic nucleus projects disynaptically, via the pontine nuclei, to the cerebellar cortex: a basal ganglia → cerebellum pathway.

methods: in vitro and in vivo synaptogenesis
finding: Cbln1 secreted by granule cells binds the N-terminal domain of the orphan receptor GluD2 on Purkinje cells; the complex is a bidirectional organizer that can induce parallel fiber synapses.

Most of the human cerebellum is functionally coupled to cerebral association networks, in proportion to their cerebral extent (primary visual cortex excepted), forming at least two mirror-image maps of the cerebrum and possibly a third.

Three mutant lines that block LTD expression (AMPA-receptor internalization) learn normally in VOR adaptation, eyeblink conditioning and Erasmus Ladder locomotion: PF–PC LTD is not essential for motor learning.
Disrupting PKC-dependent plasticity at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses impairs hippocampal place cells only when mice rely on self-motion cues, and selectively impairs path integration.
Review proposing that cerebellar learning relies on distributed, synergistic plasticity — potentiation and depression, synaptic and intrinsic, in cortex and nuclei — rather than on PF–PC LTD alone.

Heterozygous or homozygous loss of Tsc1 in Purkinje cells reduces their excitability and causes autistic-like behaviors (abnormal social interaction, repetitive behavior, vocalizations); the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin prevented both pathology and behavior.

Consensus paper reviewing cerebellar roles in speech perception, motor speech planning, verbal working memory, verbal fluency, syntax, reading and writing; the exact role of the 'linguistic cerebellum' remains debated.

Meta-analysis of more than 350 fMRI studies: the cerebellum is consistently engaged in social cognition, particularly abstract mentalizing, with clusters overlapping sensorimotor and executive territories.

Proposes that the cerebellum guides the maturation of remote neocortical circuits during sensitive periods ('developmental diaschisis'), so that early cerebellar disruption can produce the core features of autism.
Purkinje cells in zebrin-negative modules fire simple and complex spikes at higher rates than those in zebrin-positive modules; blocking TRPC3 attenuates the simple-spike difference.
The cerebellum expanded faster than predicted from neocortex size in the ape lineage, giving humans and other apes larger cerebella relative to neocortex than other anthropoid primates.

The cerebellum modulates the striatum at short latency through a disynaptic dentate→intralaminar thalamus→striatum pathway that can guide corticostriatal plasticity and, when cerebellar activity is aberrant, causes dystonia.
Review arguing that Purkinje-cell microcircuits are not uniform: zebrin-defined modules differ in molecular makeup, firing, plasticity and connectivity.

In the oculomotor vermis, Purkinje cells grouped by their complex-spike preferred direction form populations whose summed simple spikes predict saccade speed and direction in real time, although single cells do not.
Introduces a surface-based flatmap for displaying volume-averaged cerebellar imaging data; the convention behind this site's functional map.

Loss of Shank2 impairs Purkinje-cell intrinsic plasticity and PF–PC LTP and enhances inhibitory input (most in the posterior lobe), making simple spikes irregular; PC-specific knockouts show motor-learning and social-interaction deficits.

In cerebellar stroke, motor deficits follow anterior-lobe (III–VI) damage, whereas cognitive deficits follow posterior damage: language with right Crus I/II through IX, spatial with bilateral Crus I/II and right VIII, executive with VII–VIII.

All Purkinje cells, in juvenile and adult mice, have axon collaterals confined to the parasagittal plane that synapse onto other Purkinje cells, molecular-layer interneurons and Lugaro cells (not Golgi cells).
Consensus paper reviewing cerebellar contributions to emotion perception and recognition, emotional learning, the experience and regulation of emotional states, pain, and mood disorders.

Over days of eyeblink conditioning, about two-thirds of imaged granule cells acquired a response timed to match or precede the learned eyelid movement — a dense, redundant predictive signal at the input stage.

In mice, subsets of cerebellar granule cells respond to reward, reward omission or reward anticipation across multiple lobules, challenging the view that granule cells carry only sensorimotor context.

Review proposing that prediction and error-based learning, the core computations of cerebellar motor models, also operate in cognitive cerebro-cerebellar loops (attention, language, executive function, social cognition).
Network models constrained by granular-layer anatomy show that sparse synaptic connectivity (few mossy-fiber inputs per granule cell) is required for decorrelation and pattern separation.

Right Crus I: neuromodulation in typical adults altered its connectivity with inferior parietal lobule, which is atypical in children with ASD; inhibiting RCrus I Purkinje cells in mice produced ASD-like behaviors, and stimulating them rescued social deficits in PC-Tsc1 mutants.
Develops and validates the CCAS (Schmahmann syndrome) scale, a brief bedside battery that detects the executive, linguistic, visuospatial and affective deficits of cerebellar patients.

Dopamine D1 receptor-positive neurons (mostly GABAergic) form a distinct population in the lateral cerebellar nucleus, also found in human dentate; inhibiting them impairs spatial navigation memory, response inhibition, working memory and prepulse inhibition.

Review: dense disynaptic projections (subthalamic nucleus → pons → cerebellar cortex; dentate → thalamus → striatum) link the basal ganglia and cerebellum subcortically into a topographically organized network with the cerebral cortex.

The principal functional gradient runs from motor to transmodal default-mode regions; a second separates task-focused from task-unfocused regions. Motor maps are double (I–VI, VIII) and nonmotor maps triple (VI/Crus I, Crus II/VIIB, IX/X).

Molecular-layer interneurons grade climbing-fiber-evoked dendritic Ca²⁺ spikes, converting CF-mediated potentiation into depression; co-activating them with floccular climbing fibers reversed the direction of VOR adaptation.

In a flexible sensorimotor task, climbing-fiber activity is preferentially driven by correctly executed movements and reward-predicting cues — a predictive, unsigned instructive signal rather than a pure motor-error signal.

Juvenile chemogenetic perturbation of posterior-cerebellar interneurons altered adult eyeblink conditioning (paravermal VI, Crus I), reversal learning (VI), perseveration and novelty-seeking (VII) and social preference (Crus I/II); adult perturbation affected only a subset, and gait was largely spared.

Preparatory activity in frontal cortex and in the cerebellar nuclei depend on each other: silencing frontal cortex abolishes nuclear preparatory activity, and fastigial activity is needed to maintain cortical preparatory activity. Fastigial output reaches the behaviourally relevant part of frontal cortex through the thalamus, closing a cortico-cerebellar loop for motor planning (mouse).
Cerebellar nuclei send monosynaptic excitatory projections to the VTA; activating these axons is rewarding, and inhibiting them abolishes social preference.

In schizophrenia, breakdown of cerebellum–right DLPFC connectivity tracks negative-symptom severity, and TMS that restored the connectivity reduced negative symptoms in proportion to the connectivity change.

Climbing fibers signal reward expectation, delivery and omission, mapped onto microzones that are either activated or suppressed by reward; responses to predictable rewards are suppressed as mice learn.
Framework contrasting a 'universal cerebellar transform' with 'multiple functionality' across cerebellar regions, and the evidence needed to decide between them.
Dorsal hippocampus receives multisynaptic input from topographically restricted cerebellar regions, and connected regions show behavior-dependent 6–12 Hz synchronization with hippocampus.
A multi-domain task battery yields a functional parcellation of the cerebellum that outperforms resting-state parcellations; functional boundaries do not coincide with lobular boundaries.

Human cerebellar progenitor zones expand in space and time; the rhombic lip persists longer than in mouse and forms a posterior-lobule progenitor pool not seen even in macaque. Its disruption is associated with vermis hypoplasia and Dandy–Walker malformation.
Review: climbing-fiber and granule-cell signals carry predictions, rewards and expectations, suggesting cerebellar learning extends beyond supervised correction of motor errors.

Five classes of glutamatergic fastigial projection neurons, each linked to specific Purkinje-cell and olive subsets, innervate distinct targets — posturomotor, oromotor, positional-autonomic, orienting and vigilance circuits — with disynaptic links to forebrain.

Fastigial glutamatergic neurons projecting to ventrolateral PAG bidirectionally control the strength of fear memories and modulate extinction; a separate fastigial → parafascicular thalamus pathway, which may relay to the amygdala, modulates anxiety.

Circuits from Right Crus I and posterior vermis through the cerebellar nuclei and ventromedial thalamus to medial prefrontal cortex regulate social and repetitive/inflexible behavior; connectivity is disrupted in ASD-gene mouse models and people with ASD, and activating these Purkinje cells rescued behaviors in PC-Tsc1 mice.
Reconstructed to the level of individual folia, the human cerebellar surface equals ~78% of neocortical surface area, versus ~33% in the macaque.
Consensus paper: the posterior cerebellum (Crus I/II) supports social cognition, especially mentalizing and the sequencing of social actions, through connections with cerebral mentalizing networks.

Review proposing that early in learning the Purkinje-cell activity of each microzone is bound either to increase ('upbound') or to decrease ('downbound'), depending on the directional and temporal demands of its downstream circuitry and the behavior.

Each cerebellar nucleus contains a conserved set of two excitatory and three inhibitory neuron classes, duplicated during evolution; the excitatory class that targets lateral frontal cortex dominates the expanded human dentate.

Spatial and single-nucleus transcriptomics of the human fetal cerebellum map regions, transient cell types and gene-expression dynamics that differ from mouse, and locate the cell types expressing neurological-disease genes.

Whole-brain transsynaptic tracing: cerebellar outputs reach most thalamic nuclei and the neocortex; sensorimotor areas hold the most labeled neurons, but associative areas (orbital, anterior cingulate, prelimbic, infralimbic) have the highest densities.

Comprehensive cell-type atlas of the cerebellar cortex: two molecularly and functionally distinct MLI types, continuous variation in unipolar brush cells, and Purkinje-cell subtypes that are most diverse in posterior lobules.

Starting from altered cerebellar food responses in a genetic disorder of insatiable appetite (Prader–Willi syndrome), anterior deep cerebellar nuclei neurons in mice are activated by gut nutrients and end meals by raising striatal dopamine.

Probabilistic atlas of the human cerebellar lobules from 20 brains; normalizing to a cerebellum-only template (SUIT) aligns lobules better than whole-brain normalization. Its lobule maps are used for the human 3D view on this site.

Probabilistic atlas of the dentate, interposed and fastigial nuclei from 23 brains, using iron-sensitive (T2*/SWI) contrast; whole-brain normalization aligns the nuclei poorly. Its nuclei are used for the human 3D view on this site.

Cerebellar networks are reliable within a person but more variable across people than cortical networks. The frontoparietal control network is the only one over-represented in the cerebellum (2.3-fold), and cerebellar signals lag the cortex by 125–380 ms.

In two intensively scanned people, maps run from the anterior somatomotor body map to association zones at Crus I/II and back to a second body map, with a third set posteriorly. Crus I/II holds two default-network maps, several control networks and a separate language network.

A hierarchical functional atlas built from seven large task datasets, with three levels of granularity and symmetric and asymmetric versions. Combined with a short localizer scan, it predicts individual boundaries much better than group atlases.

In the same nine participants, finger tapping activates right lobules IV–V and VIII, while verb generation, mental rotation and working memory activate lobules VI and VII (Crus I/II) with prefrontal and parietal cortex.

Four segregated fronto-cerebellar circuits (motor, dorsolateral, medial and anterior prefrontal), each lateralized to the opposite cerebellar hemisphere and replicated in a second sample of 40. Prefrontal-linked territory covers much of the posterior hemispheres.

Connectivity models in which each cerebellar region pools input from several cortical areas predict cerebellar activity on new tasks best. Convergence is highest in regions for language, working memory and social cognition.

Meta-analysis of 88 PET and fMRI studies of emotion, executive function, language, music, timing and working memory. It confirms the cognitive topography of Stoodley & Schmahmann (2009) and extends it to music and timing.

Within individuals, a Crus I/II "megacluster" contains closely juxtaposed regions linked to five association networks: some respond to domain-flexible control, others to language, social or spatial/episodic demands. A smaller association cluster lies in lobule IX.

Four cerebellar regions respond to language across modalities (n = 754). One, spanning Crus I/II and VIIb, is selective for language, active in comprehension and production, sensitive to difficulty and coupled with the neocortical language network.

Tractography reconstructs crossed cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathways in vivo. About 80% of superior-peduncle streamlines link the cerebellar hemispheres, via ventrolateral thalamus, with association rather than motor cortex.

Theta-burst TMS of lateral Crus I/II changes default-network connectivity, while stimulation of vermal lobule VII changes the dorsal attention network: cerebellar regions modulate specific cortical networks.

When subjects tickle their own palm through a robot, right lateral cerebellar activity rises with the delay between movement and touch, consistent with signalling the mismatch between predicted and actual sensory consequences.

Climbing fibers fire to unexpected airpuffs and to unexpected airpuff omission, and to novel or predictive cues of other modalities: a temporal-difference prediction error like that of dopamine neurons.
Optogenetic activation of GABAergic cerebello-olivary neurons generates a negative prediction error strong enough, on its own, to extinguish conditioned eyelid responses.

Cerebellar neurons respond weakly to self-generated head motion but robustly when the motor command–movement relation is altered; their sensitivity then declines on the same time course as behavioral learning, showing an internal model being updated.
People with hereditary cerebellar ataxia adapt reaching poorly to a visuomotor perturbation. In controls, adaptation is driven by sensory prediction errors, not by online motor corrections.
On a split-belt treadmill, cerebellar damage spares reactive, feedback-driven adjustments but disrupts predictive (feedforward) locomotor adaptation.

In oculomotor vermis, error direction sets the probability of a complex spike and error magnitude its timing. A complex spike changes the next trial's simple spikes, correcting movement only along the cell's preferred error vector.

Cell-type-specific manipulations show that even subtle reductions in climbing-fiber signalling block eyeblink conditioning to natural stimuli: climbing fibers provide the essential instructive signal, although Purkinje-cell stimulation can drive learning artificially.

Nodulus/uvula Purkinje cells encode net head motion equally in active and passive movement, with no efference-copy cancellation, challenging the view that this region suppresses predictable self-motion.

Each Purkinje cell's spikes push the eye along its own vector, and the vectors add. Spikes that would push perpendicular to the movement cancel, and the population predicts when the eye reaches the goal and should stop.

Light-controlled block of AMPA-receptor endocytosis in Purkinje cells (PhotonSABER) prevents LTD and impairs adaptation of the optokinetic response and VOR, without affecting basal transmission: LTD is directly needed for this learning.
GluA2-mutant mice reported to lack LTD (yet learn normally) do show LTD with more physiological induction protocols, so these mutants do not refute the LTD theory of motor learning.

Mice lacking either parallel fiber–Purkinje LTD or interneuron feedforward inhibition still learn, but losing both severely impairs eyeblink conditioning: the two mechanisms compensate for each other.
Parallel fiber–Purkinje LTP and VOR adaptation depend on GluA3- (not GluA1-) containing AMPA receptors, whose open probability rises through cAMP and Epac rather than receptor trafficking.
Purkinje-specific SK2 deletion abolishes intrinsic plasticity but spares LTD and LTP. VOR adaptation is intact, while eyeblink conditioning is impaired.
A Purkinje cell trained by direct parallel-fiber stimulation, with interneurons blocked, learns an adaptively timed pause in firing: the timing mechanism lies in the cell itself.

Loss of one copy of Scn2a (NaV1.2) in granule cells impairs high-frequency transmission and LTP at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses, leaving the VOR hypersensitive in mice and in children with SCN2A variants. Raising Scn2a expression with CRISPR activation rescues VOR plasticity.

Climbing fibers also excite an interneuron subtype that inhibits Purkinje-targeting interneurons. Synchronous climbing fibers drive this disinhibition harder, enlarging Purkinje calcium responses, and disrupting interneuron–interneuron inhibition blocks CF-instructed motor learning.

Climbing fibers excite MLI2 interneurons by glutamate spillover; MLI2s inhibit MLI1s and so disinhibit Purkinje cells. Synchronous climbing fibers tip the balance toward MLI1 suppression, raising the dendritic calcium signals needed for LTD.

Synaptic inhibition sparsens and thresholds granule-cell sensory responses and decorrelates multisensory ensembles. Blocking it in granule cells impairs accurate cerebellum-dependent sensorimotor behavior.

Theory: the dimension of a granule-cell (or insect Kenyon-cell) representation is maximized at the small number of inputs per cell seen anatomically, so sparse connectivity can beat dense connectivity for learning.

Recordings from hundreds of granule-cell axons show high-dimensional, distributed population activity, with different behavioral states in orthogonal subspaces, as pattern-separation theories predict.
While monkeys learn new visuomotor associations, mid-lateral Purkinje-cell simple spikes report whether the last decision was rewarded; the signal fades once the association is learned.
In oculomotor cerebellum, climbing fibers (complex spikes) encode the expected reward size when the cue appears, not at reward delivery.

Review: reward expectation, delivery, size and omission are encoded by mossy-fiber and climbing-fiber pathways in a microzone-specific way. The cerebellum may combine supervised and reinforcement learning and work with the basal ganglia.

As mice learn delayed water rewards, many granule cells develop activity ramps that span the delay, and climbing fibers fire at reward. Modeled CF-dependent plasticity lets Purkinje cells ramp across seconds-long intervals.

When mice work for dopamine delivered directly into the brain, granule cells ramp predictively over the delay and climbing fibers fire after delivery. Chronic granule-cell inhibition impairs self-stimulation learning, and climbing-fiber self-stimulation alone supports moderate operant learning.

Recording oculomotor regions of both structures in the same monkeys, reward-expectation and movement signals are strongest in basal-ganglia output, intermediate in the cerebellum and weakest in the striatum.

Dentate neurons show preparatory activity like anterolateral motor cortex before reward. Silencing the dentate (by activating Purkinje cells) rapidly suppresses cortical preparatory activity, which appears to be set by a learned drop in Purkinje firing supervised by climbing-fiber reward signals.

Cerebellar degeneration abolishes temporal prediction from a single interval but spares prediction from rhythms; Parkinson's disease shows the opposite, a double dissociation of two timing mechanisms.

Review: the cerebellum implements supervised learning through input feature engineering, recurrent architecture, near-linear input–output transforms, regulated and predictive instructive signals, plasticity on multiple timescales and task-specific specializations.

Cerebellar nuclei make monosynaptic glutamatergic synapses on substantia nigra pars compacta neurons. Activating them raises striatal dopamine and locomotion; the pathway is active before movement and for reward, more so for sweeter water.

All deep cerebellar nuclei reach the dorsal striatum through the intralaminar thalamus, contacting medium spiny neurons and cholinergic interneurons; silencing the pathway alters cholinergic interneuron function.

Autoradiographic tracing: dorsolateral and medial prefrontal areas project to the basilar pons, mainly the paramedian nucleus, each with its own set of pontine targets; orbitofrontal and ventral prefrontal cortex do not. (Indexed as a review in PubMed, but it is a tracing study.)

Inhibitory neurons of the interposed and adjacent nuclei project widely to motor and sensory brainstem nuclei, not only to the inferior olive, with targets distinct from the excitatory outputs but largely shared inputs.
Purkinje cells in lobulus simplex and Crus I represent the phases, and phase differences, of prefrontal and hippocampal oscillations in a frequency- and region-specific way.
Whole-brain c-Fos network analysis: exploration recruits a cortex–basal ganglia network, while sequence-based navigation from self-motion recruits a network dominated by hippocampus and cerebellum.

Rotarod exercise engages glutamatergic dentate neurons that drive PKCδ+ amygdala neurons and reduce anxiety. On an accelerating rotarod, orexinergic hypothalamic input to the dentate adds to the effect.

The hormone asprosin activates Purkinje cells through its receptor PTPRD to increase thirst. Activating Purkinje cells triggers drinking, and deleting the receptor in Purkinje cells lowers water but not food intake, sparing motor learning and coordination.

In 983 patients and 1,349 controls from 14 samples, cerebellar grey matter is reduced in schizophrenia (d = −0.35), most in regions coupled with frontoparietal cortex. The reduction covaries with frontotemporal cortical thinning and is present in the youngest patients.

In 1,246 university students, a higher general psychopathology "p factor" goes with lower pontine white-matter integrity and a smaller left lobule VIIb, a region coupled with prefrontal control networks.

Delay eyeblink conditioning is abnormal in all five autism mouse models tested (Shank3, Mecp2, Cntnap2, Purkinje-cell Tsc1 and 15q11-13 duplication), with model-specific deficits in response probability, amplitude or timing.
Mice carrying the autism-linked 15q11-13 duplication show impaired eyeblink conditioning, dysregulated parallel fiber–Purkinje LTD and incomplete developmental elimination of surplus climbing fibers.

Abolishing granule-cell signaling impairs eyeblink conditioning and VOR learning but spares the VOR itself, anxiety and social behavior, whereas disrupting Purkinje-cell signaling impairs all of them: granule-cell input is not needed for several autism-related behaviors.

Embryonic ablation of excitatory cerebellar output neurons is largely compensated and mainly impairs motor coordination. Loss of En1/2 in the same lineage also impairs learning and spatial working memory and alters thalamo-cortico-striatal connectivity.

In essential-tremor cerebellum, climbing-fiber pruning deficits track reduced GluD2. Mice with GluD2 insufficiency develop tremor driven by CF-dependent oscillations and rescued by restoring GluD2; synchronizing Purkinje cells causes tremor, and patients show excess cerebellar oscillations.

Review of postmortem studies: essential tremor involves Purkinje-cell degeneration (axonal swellings, dendritic regression, cell loss) plus climbing-fiber and basket-cell rewiring, some of it probably compensatory.
Review: dominantly inherited spinocerebellar ataxias mostly damage Purkinje cells, through proteotoxicity, RNA toxicity and ion-channel dysfunction; no therapy yet slows them.
Randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial: two weeks of cerebello-spinal tDCS improved ataxia scores and restored cerebellar inhibition of motor cortex in neurodegenerative ataxia.

Knocking down torsinA (DYT1) in the adult cerebellum, but not the basal ganglia, causes dystonia with irregular Purkinje-cell and nuclear firing; knockdown in the immature cerebellum does not, suggesting developmental compensation.

Consensus: cerebellar dysfunction can drive dystonic movements in rodents, and human imaging and physiology implicate the cerebellum, but they do not show that it is the primary or only site of origin.
In Prrt2-mutant paroxysmal dystonia, all three nuclear cell types are active during attacks, but only activating glutamatergic nuclear neurons induces dystonia, and ablating them relieves it.

Task-force consensus: the cerebellar cognitive affective (Schmahmann) syndrome comprises executive, visuospatial, linguistic and affective deficits beyond speech; the paper reviews the evidence and therapy and lists open questions.

Review: three cognitive representations in the posterior lobe, linked with association cortex, sit apart from two sensorimotor ones. Anterior lesions cause dysmetria of movement; posterior lesions cause "dysmetria of thought" (CCAS).

Across about 47,000 adults, cerebellar aging is uneven, steepest in some association and motor regions. Larger cerebellar volume predicts better cognition with age and, in Alzheimer's disease, while amyloid burden is low, consistent with a reserve role.
GluD2-knockout mice are ataxic, form fewer parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses, keep multiple climbing fibers and lack LTD, linking synapse formation and plasticity.
Cbln1, secreted by granule cells, is needed to match and maintain parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses, to establish the climbing-fiber innervation pattern and to induce LTD; its loss mimics GluD2 loss.
Math1 fate mapping shows the rhombic lip produces cell types in temporal waves: nuclear and hindbrain neurons before E12.5, then granule-cell precursors from E12.5 to E17, anterior lobes first.
Math1 lineages from the rhombic lip form migratory streams that generate granule cells, some deep-nuclear neurons and the mossy-fiber precerebellar nuclei, but not the inferior olive.

Developmental single-nucleus atlases from human, mouse and opossum show cerebellar cell-type programs conserved for 160 million years, but early-born Purkinje-cell subtypes expanded in the human lineage and many genes changed expression.

Gene-expression and chromatin data from developing cerebellum in six mammals reveal conserved regulatory codes and human-specific regulatory changes, including a recent gain of THRB expression in cerebellar progenitors.

Comparing human, chimpanzee, macaque and marmoset cerebellar cortex, human granule cells express the sperm-receptor gene ZP2. Pontine mossy fibers induce it, and it reduces glomerular synaptic proteins and neuronal activity.

Spatial transcriptomic atlases of macaque, marmoset and mouse cerebellum reveal primate-specific Purkinje and interneuron subtypes (differing in GRID2), and gene-expression gradients that match functional-connectivity gradients.
Across mammals, relative expansion of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres evolved several times independently and tracks domain-general cognition in primates.
Across 19 mammalian species, cerebellar and cortical neuron numbers scale together, at about 3.6 cerebellar neurons per cortical neuron.
Olivocerebellar projections map onto aldolase C (zebrin) compartments in five groups, tying together the molecular, topographic and functional organization of the cerebellar cortex.

Most human Purkinje cells have several primary dendrites. In mice, about 25% of mature multibranched cells receive more than one climbing fiber, and separate dendrites can have distinct climbing-fiber receptive fields.
TRPC3 controls simple-spike firing only in zebrin-negative Purkinje cells. Losing it impairs eyeblink conditioning (zebrin− modules) but spares compensatory eye-movement adaptation (zebrin+ modules).

Single-cell transcriptomes of 25 medulloblastomas: SHH tumors resemble granule neurons at different stages, Group 3 and 4 tumors follow progenitor-to-neuron trajectories, and cross-species comparison points to distinct glutamatergic cells of origin.
A human rhombic-lip lineage with photoreceptor and unipolar-brush-cell signatures matches Group 3 and Group 4 medulloblastoma, and imaging places these tumors at the nodulus.

Group 4 medulloblastoma resembles early progenitors of the human rhombic-lip subventricular zone, stalled by mutations converging on the CBFA complex; knocking down OTX2 releases the block. The expanded human rhombic lip may predispose our species.

Exome sequencing of 282 people from 100 families with Dandy–Walker malformation or cerebellar hypoplasia gives a diagnosis in 36 families (51% for hypoplasia, 16% for Dandy–Walker), implicates vascular development (PDGFRB) and confirms large non-genetic prenatal contributions.

Review: cerebellar injury and underdevelopment, especially of the external granular layer, are common in very premature infants and likely contribute to later cognitive, behavioral, attentional and social deficits.

In preterm infants, cerebellar growth and later outcomes scale with gestational age at birth. Postmortem spatial transcriptomics shows incomplete granule-cell maturation and impaired Purkinje-cell refinement: prematurity displaces cerebellar maturation.
Consensus review of cerebellar development: progenitor zones and their neurogenic strategies, fate-specification programs, the stages of cortical organization, and developmental disorders.
Review: the cerebellum's protracted development widens its window of vulnerability; intellectual disability, autism, ADHD and Down syndrome have been linked to abnormal cerebellar development.

Noradrenaline acts on α2-adrenergic receptors to lower the release probability of climbing-fiber synapses, which shrinks climbing-fiber-evoked dendritic Ca²⁺ signals and reduces short- and long-term associative plasticity at parallel-fiber synapses (rat).

Review and theory: proposes that serotonin controls the 'responsibility' of each microcomplex, noradrenaline gates unsupervised learning in the cerebellar cortex, dopamine enhances goal-oriented learning, and acetylcholine sets the speed of supervised learning in Purkinje cells.

Infusing the β-adrenergic blocker propranolol into lobule HVI and the interpositus impaired acquisition of conditioned eyeblink responses, and a PKA inhibitor prevented it; neither drug affected established responses (rat).
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): activating the pathway from the locus coeruleus to rat Purkinje cells gave pharmacological evidence that it is a noradrenergic inhibitory input.
Noradrenaline acting on β2-adrenergic receptors raises cAMP in basket cells, depolarizing them and increasing their firing, which facilitates GABAergic IPSCs onto Purkinje cells (rat slices).

Rabies-based input mapping shows that locus coeruleus noradrenaline neurons receive input from many regions, including cerebellar Purkinje cells, and LC neurons that project to one output region also project to all other regions examined (mouse).

Noxious stimuli release noradrenaline from locus coeruleus terminals in the cerebellar cortex, and Bergmann glia integrate it as α1-adrenergic Ca²⁺ 'flares'. Silencing LC terminals or Bergmann glia, or knocking down glial α1 receptors, reduced nocifensive licking and neuropathic pain; activating Bergmann glia lowered Purkinje firing (mouse).

In tottering mice, a model of episodic ataxia type 2, stress-released noradrenaline acts on Purkinje-cell α1-adrenergic receptors and, through casein kinase 2 (likely reducing Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channel activity), disrupts pacemaking; the erratic firing triggers motor attacks, which blocking the cascade prevents.

Serotonin selectively excites Lugaro cells, which inhibit Golgi cells; each Lugaro cell's transverse axon contacts more than 100 Golgi cells, so serotonin can control inhibition in the granular layer (rat slices).

Granule-cell 5-HT3 receptors regulate Purkinje-cell maturation through reelin: in 5-HT3A knockout mice, Purkinje cells mature early and climbing-fiber elimination is delayed, within a specific developmental window.

During the first three postnatal weeks, granule cells express functional 5-HT3 receptors, including presynaptically at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses, where they modulate paired-pulse plasticity (mouse).

About two-thirds of labeled Lugaro cells are GABA/glycinergic; they receive serotonergic fibers and innervate molecular-layer interneurons and Golgi cells but not Purkinje cells. Their dendrites and ascending axons stay within aldolase C compartments, whereas transverse axons cross several (mouse).

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 19 patients with cerebellar cortical atrophy, the 5-HT1A agonist buspirone improved the kinetic ataxia score and the maximum time standing with feet together; the effect was partial and not clinically major.

Serotonin depolarizes Golgi cells (likely via 5-HT2A receptors) without acting directly on granule cells or mossy fibers; the extra tonic inhibition lowers granule-cell spike probability without changing spike timing (rat slices).

Dopamine D2 receptors are preferentially expressed by Purkinje cells, where they regulate synaptic efficacy; changing Purkinje-cell D2R levels in adult male mice altered sociability and preference for social novelty without affecting motor function.

Review: the cerebellum contains high dopamine levels, receives midbrain dopaminergic afferents and expresses all dopamine receptor subtypes (D1–D5); the cerebellar dopamine system may matter in Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia.

Purkinje cells express D3 receptors, VMAT2 and the dopamine transporter, most strongly in lobules IX–X; the depolarization-induced slow current (DISC) depends on Ca²⁺-dependent release of vesicular dopamine from Purkinje cells acting back on them (mouse).

Bergmann glia express D1 receptors, and Purkinje cells make dopamine (via cytochrome P450) and release it in an activity-dependent way; glial D1R activation depolarizes Bergmann glia and releases Ca²⁺, altering Purkinje-cell excitatory and inhibitory input, and deleting glial D1R reduces locomotion and social activity (mouse).

Cholinergic markers are sparse and vary between species and lobules. The predominant fiber system that may use acetylcholine is mossy fibers from the vestibular nuclei to the nodulus and ventral uvula, which contact granule cells and unipolar brush cells, probably through nicotinic receptors. Beaded cholinergic fibers from the pedunculopontine tegmental and lateral paragigantocellular nuclei, and to a lesser extent raphe nuclei, reach the cortex and nuclei (rat; receptors also mapped in rabbit, cat and monkey).

Golgi cells express nicotinic and muscarinic receptors; optogenetically released acetylcholine hyperpolarizes them, cutting tonic and evoked inhibition of granule cells, while presynaptic muscarinic receptors reduce mossy-fiber glutamate release. Granule-cell spiking rises or falls depending on each cell's balance of excitation and inhibition.

α7 nicotinic receptors on mossy-fiber terminals and granule-cell dendrites let weak mossy-fiber bursts, which would otherwise cause LTD, induce LTP at mossy fiber–granule cell synapses, also in vivo; activating α7 receptors in the flocculus impairs VOR adaptation.

Review of the cerebellar cholinergic system, a third type of afferent after climbing and mossy fibers: its origins, receptor distribution, effects on firing and plasticity, changes with development and aging, and links to ataxia and autism.

Lesion experiments show that most, if not all, cerebellar nicotinic receptors are on cells intrinsic to the cerebellum rather than on afferents; β4- (not β2-) containing receptors regulate inhibitory synaptic efficacy at two major classes of cerebellar neurons (rat).

In interpositus neurons, the cholinergic agonist carbachol transiently raised firing, induced long-term depression of IPSCs and short-term depression of EPSCs, all through muscarinic receptors (rat slices).

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in SCA3, the α4β2 nicotinic partial agonist varenicline improved axial measures (gait, stance, rapid alternating movements) and timed walk; the total ataxia score showed only a trend (Class II evidence).

Histamine microinjected into the interpositus nucleus improved rotarod and balance-beam performance through H2 receptors; the H2 antagonist ranitidine impaired performance, whereas an H1 antagonist had no effect (rat).

Histamine depolarizes glutamatergic and glycinergic projection neurons, but not interneurons, of the cerebellar nuclei via H2 receptors coupled to HCN channels; blocking HCN channels to block endogenous histaminergic input impairs motor balance and coordination (rat).

Review of direct, bidirectional cerebellar–hypothalamic projections: hypothalamic fibers, some of them histaminergic, end in the cerebellar cortex and nuclei and excite neurons through H2 and/or H1 receptors, and all cerebellar nuclei project back to the hypothalamus.

Review: histaminergic afferents from the hypothalamic tuberomammillary nucleus extend fine varicose fibers throughout the cerebellar cortex and nuclei, and histamine directly excites Purkinje cells, granule cells and nuclear neurons, influencing motor balance and coordination.

Orexinergic hypothalamic fibers excite Purkinje cells of the flocculus folium-p, which projects to the parabrachial nucleus; an orexin antagonist attenuated the blood-flow redistribution of the defense reaction (rabbit).
Orexin-A and orexin-B excite interpositus neurons through OX2 receptors (rat slices).

Orexin-A fibers from perifornical and lateral hypothalamic neurons reach the vestibular nuclei and the cerebellar nuclei (densest in the fastigial nucleus, sparser in interposed and dentate), with a few in paraflocculus cortex; OX1-receptor-like immunoreactivity is found in these nuclei and in the paraflocculus granular layer (rat).

Review: more than 30 neuropeptides occur in cerebellar cells and circuits, where they tune excitability, transmission, plasticity and development; it details eight (BDNF, CRF, angiotensin II, NPY, orexin, TRH, oxytocin and secretin) as candidate therapeutic targets in ataxias and psychiatric disorders.

Corticotropin-releasing factor from climbing fibers is permissive for parallel fiber–Purkinje LTD via PKC: CRF antagonists block LTD, and cerebella deprived of climbing fibers lack LTD until CRF is supplied (rat).

CRF is very highly expressed throughout the inferior olive. Reducing olivary CRF causes motor deficits under challenging conditions without changing basal locomotion or anxiety-like behavior, and chronic social defeat stress persistently lowers it (mouse).

CRF-expressing olivary neurons project to the cerebellar nuclei, where CRF excites glutamatergic interpositus projection neurons through CRF1 and CRF2 receptors (Kir and HCN channels); olivo-cerebellar CRF deficiency causes ataxia-like deficits that CRF rescues (rat).
CRF raises Purkinje-cell firing by shifting the activation of persistent Na⁺ and hyperpolarization-activated (Ih) currents and activating voltage-dependent K⁺ current (rat slices).

In anesthetized mice, CRF applied to the molecular layer raised Purkinje simple-spike rates (partly via CRF1 and CRF2 receptors) and increased mEPSC frequency through presynaptic CRF2 receptors and PKA.
Activating CRF2 receptors, present on climbing-fiber afferents, enhances complex spikes and climbing fiber–Purkinje transmission through a presynaptic PKA pathway (mouse).

Rats given CRF directly into the cerebellum performed better on the rotarod, especially early in training, whereas a CRF-receptor antagonist reduced endurance on the rod; the authors infer a role for endogenous CRF in cerebellar motor learning.
CGRP is transiently present in developing climbing fibers; its receptor is mainly astrocytic, and CGRP triggers Ca²⁺ signals in Bergmann glia (mouse).
CGRP stimulates dendritic growth of Purkinje cells in culture, likely acting through astrocytes (rat).

Brief depolarization of Purkinje cells suppresses parallel- and climbing-fiber EPSCs for tens of seconds by releasing endogenous cannabinoids that act on presynaptic CB1 receptors and reduce presynaptic Ca²⁺ influx (depolarization-induced suppression of excitation; rat).

Activating mGluR1 on Purkinje cells releases endocannabinoids that act on presynaptic cannabinoid receptors to depress climbing-fiber input, without needing a postsynaptic Ca²⁺ rise; depolarization-evoked Ca²⁺ transients and repetitive parallel-fiber stimulation also trigger this retrograde inhibition.

Parallel fiber–Purkinje LTD requires the endocannabinoid 2-AG and CB1 receptors: a CB1 antagonist or blocking 2-AG synthesis prevents it, and it is absent in CB1-knockout mice. Purkinje cells release 2-AG that both transiently inhibits release and induces a postsynaptic LTD.
CB1-knockout mice, and mice given a CB1 antagonist, are impaired in acquiring delay, but not trace, eyeblink conditioning.

Review: endocannabinoids released from postsynaptic neurons act on presynaptic CB1 receptors to reduce transmitter release transiently or for long periods, a form of retrograde signaling discovered in 2001.
Deleting CB1 receptors from granule cells abolished endocannabinoid-mediated short-term plasticity at parallel-fiber synapses and parallel fiber LTD (mouse).
The delay-eyeblink deficit of CB1-knockout mice stems from their reduced locomotor activity: treadmill walking rescues learning, and granule-cell-specific CB1 knockouts learn normally (mouse).
Locomotor activity enhances delay eyeblink conditioning in mice, an effect mediated by increased mossy-fiber activity.

Review: cerebellar endocannabinoid signaling (mainly via CB1) must stay balanced for motor coordination; activating it causes ataxia-like deficits that CB1 antagonists prevent, CB1 deficits can cause progressive ataxia, and cannabinoid-based therapy for ataxias is discussed.

Climbing-fiber stimulation releases nitric oxide in cerebellar slices; hemoglobin or the NOS inhibitor L-NMMA blocks LTD, and NO or cGMP can substitute for climbing-fiber stimulation in inducing it (rat).

Stimulating parallel fibers at 1 Hz induces a postsynaptically expressed LTP that depends on nitric oxide but not cAMP or cGMP and is enhanced by chelating postsynaptic Ca²⁺, a plausible counterpart to LTD.
LTD requires nitric oxide coinciding with depolarization-induced postsynaptic Ca²⁺ rise; NO acts as an anterograde messenger.
NMDA receptors on molecular-layer interneurons, not on granule or Purkinje cells, are required for parallel fiber LTD and horizontal OKR adaptation; a nitric-oxide donor restores LTD (mouse).

Short stimulus trains in the molecular layer release adenosine (TTX- and Ca²⁺-sensitive), probably from parallel fibers, and the adenosine feeds back to inhibit parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission (rat).

Bergmann-glia Ca²⁺ responses to molecular-layer stimulation have a fast AMPA-receptor phase and a P2 purinergic phase that releases Ca²⁺ from stores; molecular-layer interneurons are the likely ATP source (rat).

In the immature cerebellum, Bergmann glia release D-serine, which binds GluD2 to drive AMPA-receptor endocytosis and LTD; mice whose GluD2 lacks the D-serine site have impaired LTD and motor dyscoordination during development.
μ- and δ- (but not κ-) opioid receptors on parallel-fiber terminals reduce glutamate release onto Purkinje cells, and endogenous opioid peptides at these synapses also inhibit release (mouse slices).
The μ-opioid agonist DAMGO depresses parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission presynaptically, through PKA and MEK signaling (mouse).
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): enkephalin immunoreactivity is found in Golgi cells and mossy fibers of the cerebellum of mammals, birds, amphibians and teleost fish.

Rostral anterior cingulate neurons that project to the pontine nucleus mediate placebo analgesia: inhibiting them disrupts it and activating them produces analgesia. Pontine neurons are rich in opioid receptors, and Purkinje cells show similar activity during expectation of pain relief (mouse).

Cerebellar oxytocin-receptor expression patterns vary widely between knock-in reporter lines. In Oxtr-Cre reporter mice, expression in Bergmann glia was more variable than in Purkinje cells, and physical damage with inflammation selectively upregulated the receptor in Bergmann glia (mouse).

Cerebellar RNA-seq of SCA1 mouse models: in ATXN1[30Q]D776 mice, which are ataxic without progressive Purkinje-cell pathology, cholecystokinin (Cck) is upregulated, and its action on Cck1 receptors likely explains the lack of progressive pathology.

Removing Cck1 receptors from ATXN1[30Q]D776 mice causes progressive disease with Purkinje-cell death. The Cck1R agonist A71623 dampened Purkinje-cell pathology and motor deficits in SCA1 mice, improved motor performance in SCA2 mice, and corrected mTORC1 signaling.
Intranasal neuropeptide Y alleviated motor deficits and neuropathology in a mouse model of Machado–Joseph disease (SCA3).

Exogenous PACAP slows granule-cell migration in the external granular and molecular layers, whereas blocking endogenous PACAP speeds migration in the Purkinje-cell layer, a transient, layer-specific brake (early postnatal mice).

Estradiol enhances parallel fiber–Purkinje LTP (not LTD) and increases parallel-fiber synapse density; acting on Purkinje-cell estrogen receptor β, it improves gain-decrease adaptation of the VOR (mouse).

In mouse cerebellum, estrogen-receptor activation of mGluR1a strongly enhances parallel fiber–Purkinje transmission. Blocking local (aromatase-dependent) estrogen synthesis weakens it, lowering estrogen impairs locomotor performance, and the facilitation occurs in both sexes.

Mice with a dominant-negative thyroid-hormone receptor in Purkinje cells have impaired motor coordination and learning; in them, LTD-inducing stimulation produces LTP, with smaller dendritic Ca²⁺ signals and less SERCA2 and IP3R1. Adult-onset thyroid-hormone deficiency does not do this, so the effect is developmental.
Many fastigial premotor neurons are glycinergic and project ipsilaterally to vestibular and reticular nuclei (mouse).
Lugaro cell → Golgi cell IPSCs are mixed GABAergic–glycinergic, whereas basket and stellate cell inputs to Golgi cells are purely GABAergic (rat).
A population of GABA-glycinergic cerebellar nuclear neurons projects to the cerebellar cortex and inhibits a subpopulation of GABAergic Golgi cells (mouse).
Nuclear interneurons contact principal neurons through glycine-receptor-rich synapses that carry about 15% of the IPSC, whereas glycine receptors carry under 3% of Purkinje-cell IPSCs (mouse).
Input to the inferior olive from the cerebellar nuclei is asynchronous and purely GABAergic, whereas vestibular-nucleus input is synchronous and mixed GABA/glycine (mouse).

Serotonergic fibers reach all layers of the cerebellar cortex, with lobular variation; double labeling traced them almost exclusively to the gigantocellular, paragigantocellular and pontine (oralis) reticular nuclei, mostly not to the raphe nuclei (rat).

Dopaminergic VTA neurons project to the cerebellar cortex (granular and Purkinje-cell layers, mainly Crus I and paraflocculus), non-dopaminergic VTA neurons project to the lateral and interpositus nuclei, and the VTA receives input from these nuclei (rat).

Familial hemiplegic migraine and episodic ataxia type 2 are allelic channelopathies of CACNL1A4 (CACNA1A), the brain-specific P/Q-type Ca²⁺-channel α1 subunit: FHM families carry missense mutations, and EA-2 families carry mutations that disrupt the reading frame.

In mouse motor cortex, the laminar connectivity matrix is dominated by layer 2 outflow to deeper layers, and stimulating upper but not lower layers evokes network-wide events in disinhibited slices: descending excitation from upper-layer neurons drives the output neurons of the lower layers.

Each long-range input to mouse vibrissal M1 has its own laminar profile: orbital cortex targets L6; M2 targets mainly L5B, including pyramidal-tract neurons; VA/VL motor thalamus targets L2/3 through L5B but avoids L6; POm and barrel cortex target only the upper layers (L2/3 and L5A).

methods: synaptic circuit mapping of projection-identified neurons
finding: The main excitatory pathway of mouse motor cortex, layer 2/3 → 5, splits into pathways to corticospinal neurons in upper layer 5B and corticostriatal neurons in lower layer 5A; connectivity depends on both sublayer position and long-range projection target.

Two types of pyramidal-tract neuron, both projecting to basal ganglia and brainstem targets: one projects to thalamic regions that connect back to motor cortex and carries early preparatory activity that lasts until movement starts; the other projects to medullary motor centres and mainly carries late preparatory activity and motor commands.

An anterior lateral region of mouse cortex (a possible homologue of primate premotor cortex) holds intermingled neurons predicting ipsi- or contralateral movements in equal proportions, yet unilateral inactivation during planning disrupts contralateral movements. Layer 5 neurons projecting within the cortex have unbiased laterality; a contralateral bias arises only in brainstem-projecting layer 5 neurons, late in planning.

In a whisker-based decision task with a short-term memory period, barrel cortex was critical for sensation, while unilateral inhibition of anterior lateral motor cortex during the memory period biased licking responses to the ipsilateral side; motor cortex showed choice-specific preparatory activity, suggesting serial flow from sensory to motor areas (mouse).

During a mouse prehension task, inactivating the thalamus perturbed motor cortex activity and limb kinematics at any stage of the movement, and both thalamic activity and the current cortical state predicted cortical activity: the pattern generator for dexterous arm movement is input-driven and distributed across strongly interacting regions.

In rats trained on a task requiring spatiotemporally precise movement patterns but no dexterity, motor cortex lesions after training left the learned skill intact, whereas lesions before training prevented its acquisition, suggesting that motor cortex 'tutors' subcortical circuits that execute the skill.

Imaging the same layer 2/3 neurons of mouse motor cortex over two weeks of lever-press learning: inhibitory activity stays relatively stable, while excitatory activity first expands and explores, then refines into a smaller population with reproducible spatiotemporal sequences unique to experts, coinciding with a transient increase in spine turnover.

Forelimb reach training forms new dendritic spines on output pyramidal neurons of the contralateral motor cortex within an hour; the new spines are preferentially stabilized and endure after training stops, pre-existing spines are gradually eliminated, and different skills are encoded by different sets of synapses (mouse).

Learning and novel sensory experience drive protracted spine formation and elimination in mouse cortex, and the extent of remodeling correlates with behavioral improvement; a small fraction of new spines, together with most spines formed early in development, persists for life.

After motor skill learning, synapses of horizontal connections in trained rat motor cortex (MI) are near the ceiling of their modification range: LTP is markedly reduced and LTD enhanced, while the range itself is unchanged, consistent with learning strengthening synapses through LTP.

Motor cortex population responses during reaching contain a brief but strong oscillatory component whose amplitude and phase follow from the preparatory state, suggesting a mechanistic role for preparatory activity and explaining many confusing features of single-neuron responses (monkey).

Arm-area motor cortex neurons are only broadly tuned to movement direction in three-dimensional space, but the vector sum of their preferred directions, each weighted by the cell's activity (the population vector), points in the direction of movement (monkey).

Of 323 task-related arm-area motor cortex cells, 241 (74.6%) varied their discharge with movement direction along a bell-shaped tuning curve (sinusoidal in about 75% of them), already before EMG onset; overlapping tuning curves suggest that direction is coded by a population of cells (monkey).

Rabies tracing from single muscles in rhesus monkeys divides M1 in two: a rostral 'old' M1 without cortico-motoneuronal (CM) cells, standard for many mammals, and a caudal 'new' M1 whose CM cells contact shoulder, elbow and finger motoneurons monosynaptically, present only in some higher primates and humans.

Review: descending motor pathways differ widely across species, for example in how corticospinal signals reach upper-limb motoneurons; direct cortico-motoneuronal (CM) connections operate in parallel with less direct routes, and their influence is significant and may serve adaptive movements of the distal extremities.

Single neurons in the monkey M1 hand area are active with movements of different fingers, and the populations active for different fingers overlap extensively: control of any finger uses neurons distributed throughout the hand area rather than a somatotopically segregated population.

Stimulating monkey primary motor and premotor cortex with 500-ms trains evokes coordinated postures involving many joints (for example, the hand shaped into a grip and brought to the open mouth), reached from any starting position; arm postures are arranged across cortex as a map of hand positions around the body that spans both areas.

Precision fMRI shows the classic M1 homunculus interrupted by inter-effector regions that alternate with foot, hand and mouth areas; they have thinner cortex, strong connectivity to each other and to the cingulo-opercular network, and co-activate during action planning and axial movements, forming a somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) (human; macaque and infant data suggest homologues and precursors).

fMRI localizes the motor hand area to a knob-like segment of the precentral gyrus, omega- or epsilon-shaped in axial section, which corresponds to the 'middle knee' of the central sulcus and is a reliable landmark for identifying the precentral gyrus (human).

A multimodal cell census of primary motor cortex integrates single-cell transcriptomes, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, spatial transcriptomics, morphology, physiology and input-output mapping into a consensus taxonomy of cell types conserved from mouse to marmoset and human, with a genetic toolset for targeting glutamatergic types.

Profiling more than 450,000 M1 nuclei from humans, marmosets and mice shows a broadly conserved cellular makeup with species specializations in cell-type proportions, gene expression, DNA methylation and chromatin state; few marker genes are conserved, and patch-seq identifies layer 5 corticospinal Betz cells in non-human primates and humans and characterizes their specialized physiology and anatomy.

Comparing purified corticospinal motor neurons (CSMN) with callosal and corticotectal projection neurons across development identifies genes specific to each population; null mutants show that Ctip2 (Bcl11b) is critical for the development of CSMN axonal projections to the spinal cord (mouse).

Fezl is required for the specification of corticospinal motor neurons and other subcerebral projection neurons: they are absent from Fezl-null neocortex without increased cell death or migration defects, other neurons are born normally, and overexpression of Fezl produces excess subcerebral projection neurons (mouse).

In Fezl-deficient mice, layer 5 projection neurons show molecular, morphological and axon-targeting defects: the corticospinal tract is absent, corticotectal and pontine projections are severely reduced, and Ctip2, a transcription factor required for corticospinal tract formation, is not expressed.

Dopaminergic terminals in rat M1 originate in the VTA. VTA stimulation induces c-fos in M1, blocked by intracortical D1 and D2 antagonists; destroying VTA dopamine neurons prevents improvement in skilled reaching, which recovers with levodopa given into M1, while performance of an already learned skill is unaffected.

In rat M1, eliminating dopaminergic terminals impairs acquisition of a motor skill (restored by dopamine substitution) but not execution of a learned one, and reversible D1/D2 receptor blockade temporarily impairs acquisition and reduces LTP within M1.

Selective lesions of the basal forebrain cholinergic system disrupt the cortical map reorganization that accompanies learning a skilled motor task and impair that learning, without impairing associative fear learning or overall sensorimotor function (rat).

In healthy people, training-dependent increases in motor-evoked potential amplitude and motor map reorganization, measured with TMS, are reduced in carriers of the BDNF val66met polymorphism, suggesting that BDNF is involved in experience-dependent plasticity of human motor cortex.

After stroke in mice, tonic inhibition in the peri-infarct zone rises through extrasynaptic GABA(A) receptors because GABA transporter (GAT-3/GAT-4) function is impaired; an α5-selective inverse agonist given at a delay after stroke, or genetically lowering α5- or δ-subunit receptors, promotes early and sustained recovery of motor function.

In 21 chronic stroke patients with upper-limb impairment, those with motor-evoked potentials to TMS could still make meaningful gains 3 years after stroke; in those without, functional potential fell with corticospinal tract disruption, with no meaningful gains once internal-capsule FA asymmetry exceeded 0.25.

Threshold-tracking TMS in 23 patients with motor neuron disease shows reduced short-interval intracortical inhibition, most marked with less severe disease but present even in advanced disease, along with other signs of cortical hyperexcitability; upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction coexist, and cortical hyperexcitability is an early feature.

In a person with tetraplegia, a 96-microelectrode array in primary motor cortex showed that intended hand motion still modulated spiking three years after spinal cord injury; decoded activity drove a 'neural cursor' to open e-mail and operate devices, opened and closed a prosthetic hand, and performed rudimentary actions with a robotic arm.

An intracortical BCI decoded attempted handwriting from motor cortex activity with a recurrent neural network, letting a participant whose hand was paralysed by spinal cord injury type 90 characters per minute with 94.1% raw online accuracy (above 99% offline with autocorrect); temporally complex movements may be easier to decode than point-to-point ones.

After a small ischemic infarct in the hand representation of squirrel monkey motor cortex, retraining of skilled hand use prevented the loss of hand territory in the adjacent undamaged cortex (sometimes the hand area expanded into former elbow and shoulder regions), together with behavioral recovery of skilled hand function.

Microstimulation maps of squirrel monkey M1 change with use: digit training expands digit representations and shrinks wrist/forearm zones, forearm training in a key-turning task does the reverse, the changes are progressive and reversible, and movement combinations used together come to be represented together.

By week 4 of daily practice of a finger-movement sequence, the extent of M1 activated (BOLD fMRI) by the practised sequence enlarged relative to an unpractised one and stayed so for several months; within the first session, repetition first reduced and later enlarged the activated area (human).

Retrograde tracing from the cervical spinal cord in macaques labels corticospinal neurons in M1 and in six premotor areas (in area 6 on the lateral and medial surfaces and in areas 23 and 24 of the cingulate sulcus); the premotor arm areas hold as many or more corticospinal neurons as the arm area of M1 and make up more than 60% of the frontal cortex that projects to the spinal cord.

In monkeys performing memorized movement sequences, some supplementary motor area cells fire exclusively for a sequence of movements performed in a particular order, activity not found in primary motor cortex, suggesting a signal for planning several movements ahead.

Mouse corticospinal neurons are required for skilled food-pellet retrieval and fire as sequentially activated, topographically ordered ensembles; neurons of the caudal forelimb area control reaching and those of the rostral area grasping (both are needed for pronation), and they terminate at different spinal levels on premotor neurons of different muscles.

Corticospinal fibers from mouse motor cortex synapse directly onto spinal premotor interneurons, including Chx10+ cells; motor cortex lesions or silencing Chx10+ interneurons impair skilled reaching. Corticospinal neurons of sensory cortex do not contact premotor interneurons directly and prefer Vglut3+ interneurons; sensory-cortex lesions or inhibiting Vglut3+ interneurons impair food-pellet release.

Sudden optogenetic inhibition of mouse cortex blocked initiation or froze execution of a learned reach-grab-eat behavior but left untrained forelimb movements unaffected; kinematically normal 'rebound' prehension followed the end of inhibition in trained, food-deprived mice: cortical activity is necessary and sufficient for enacting this learned skill.

During movement preparation, while the monkey holds still, changes in motor cortical activity cancel out at the level of the population readouts that drive muscles ('output-null' patterns), so motor cortex can prepare without moving; evidence suggests the same mechanism operates in dorsal premotor cortex, largely accounting for the attenuation of preparatory activity in primary motor cortex.

During motor learning in mice, spine reorganization of layer 2/3 excitatory neurons occurs on distal apical dendrites in L1, not perisomatic dendrites; SOM interneuron boutons drop as training begins while PV boutons gradually rise, and enhancing or suppressing SOM activity during training destabilizes or hyperstabilizes spines and impairs learning of stereotyped movements.

In non-human primates, thalamic input to motor cortex (studied in the cerebellar-thalamocortical system) triggers feedforward inhibition by contacting inhibitory cells through highly effective GluR2-lacking AMPA receptors, and the movement-related activity of PV interneurons precedes the firing of pyramidal cells, which may amplify the cortical effect of cerebellar signals.

Single-neuron tracing in the rat ventral anterior-ventral lateral motor thalamus: neurons of a rostromedial zone dominated by inhibitory afferents project to cortex and striatum, with 47-66% of their varicosities in layer I, whereas neurons of a caudolateral zone dominated by excitatory subcortical afferents project almost only to cortex, mostly to middle layers, suggesting that basal ganglia and cerebellar signals reach apical and basal dendrites, respectively.

Review: neurons in motor cortex and connected regions fire in anticipation of specific movements long before they occur; large-scale recordings and quantified perturbations in rodents reveal a network distributed across multiple brain regions that collectively supports motor planning.

Review: decades of encoding and decoding studies of movement tuning in motor cortex have not produced an agreed-upon framework; a dynamical systems perspective asks how the current population response determines the future one and may unify how neural activity relates to movement parameters.

Corticospinal neurons lose their regrowth potential after development, together with a fall in mTOR activity that axon injury lowers further; conditionally deleting Pten, a negative regulator of mTOR, enhanced sprouting of uninjured corticospinal axons and let a cohort of injured ones regenerate past a spinal cord lesion and re-form synapses (mouse).

In rat M1 slices, thalamocortical input excites corticospinal neurons for distal and proximal forelimb equally before learning, but after skilled grasp training it is biased toward distal-forelimb neurons, with a cell-specific increase in mEPSC amplitude but not in presynaptic release probability.

Review: ideas about motor cortex were shaped by stimulation-evoked motor maps, but volitional control entails both initiating movements and suppressing undesired ones; classic and recent findings show that motor cortex neurons have a role in both.

Like ALM neurons, thalamic neurons showed selective persistent delay activity that predicted movement direction. Unilateral photoinhibition of delay activity in either produced contralesional neglect; photoinhibiting the thalamus caused a short-latency, near-complete collapse of ALM activity, and photoinhibiting ALM diminished thalamic activity, suggesting that persistent activity requires reciprocal excitation across multiple brain areas (mouse).

In auditory and tactile delayed-response tasks with directional licking, ALM preparatory activity had similar features: most neurons were direction-selective, with spatially intermingled neurons preferring either direction; many mixed coding of sensory stimulus and licking direction, biased toward direction; delay activity was monotonic and low-dimensional; and pairs with similar direction selectivity had high spike-count correlations (mouse).

During the delay epoch of a delayed-response task, the activity of ALM neurons moved toward discrete end points corresponding to specific movement directions. The end points were robust to transient optogenetic perturbations, which occasionally switched population activity to the other end point, followed by incorrect actions: discrete attractor dynamics underlie short-term memory related to motor planning (mouse).

Ascending glutamatergic neurons in the midbrain reticular and pedunculopontine nuclei showed short-latency, phasic changes in firing selective for an auditory Go cue. The signal is transmitted via the thalamus to motor cortex, where it triggers a rapid reorganization from planning-related activity to a motor command that drives directional licking (mouse).

Review: joint experimental and computational studies using rapid, calibrated perturbations show that cortical dynamics during motor planning reflect fixed points of neural activity (attractors); subcortical control signals reshape and move these attractors over multiple timescales, causing commitment to specific actions and rapid transitions to movement execution.

Recordings with multiple Neuropixels probes from loops connected to ALM during memory-guided directional licking: neurons encoding stimuli, choices and actions were distributed across the brain, but choice coding was concentrated in ALM and subcortical areas receiving ALM input, in an ALM-dependent manner. Choice signals appeared first in ALM and the midbrain, then in the thalamus and other areas; at movement initiation, choice-selective activity collapsed across the brain, followed by new activity patterns driving specific actions (mouse).

In frontal-cortex neurons of mice performing a decision-making task, standard fluctuation-driven network models accounted for spiking statistics but not the heterogeneity of sub-threshold membrane potentials. To address this, the authors incorporated dendritic morphology into the models, where dendrites increased neuronal selectivity and reduced error trials. The authors suggest that, during decision-making, neurons in high-order cortical areas operate in a fluctuation-driven regime (mouse; models).

In a flexible lick-timing task, after transient silencing of the frontal cortex, cortical and striatal activity swiftly returned to pre-silencing levels and resumed ramping, shifting lick timing by about the silencing duration; brief striatal inhibition instead gradually decreased ramping in both regions, which resumed from post-inhibition levels and shifted lick timing beyond the inhibition. Inhibiting frontal cortex thus paused this timer and inhibiting striatum rewound it, consistent with the striatum being part of a network that integrates frontal-cortex input into ramping activity that regulates motor timing (mouse).

In mice learning a motor timing task, transient CaMKII inactivation in premotor cortex impaired learning without affecting execution of learned actions. CaMKII-dependent plasticity in two pyramidal tract (PT) subtypes, but not in intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, was required for learning: CaMKII activity in the two PT subtypes was necessary to shape distinct aspects of premotor dynamics that jointly anticipate motor timing, whereas IT plasticity was required to reduce the dimensionality of cortical activity (mouse).

Benchmarking optogenetic inactivation of small neocortical regions: exciting GABAergic neurons inactivated more effectively than light-gated ion pumps, and transgenic mice expressing GtACR1 gave the most potent inactivation. Inactivation generally spread substantially beyond the light, owing to strong coupling between cortical neurons, and its offset was followed by light dose-dependent rebound excitation, limiting temporal resolution (mouse).

Neurons in the monkey prefrontal cortex and in the nucleus medialis dorsalis of the thalamus changed their firing during a delayed-response test: most increased firing during the cue or at the start of the delay, and some fired above their intertrial rate throughout the delay. The authors interpret this as suggestive evidence that frontothalamic circuits support the attentive process involved in short-term memory.

In an oculomotor delayed-response task, 87 of 288 neurons in and around the principal sulcus changed their activity during the delay; for 79% of them the delay activity was directional, occurring only after cues in a certain range of visual-field directions, and the preferences held across delays of 1-6 s (monkey).

Local injections of the selective D1 dopamine receptor antagonists SCH23390 and SCH39166 into prefrontal cortex caused dose-dependent, delay-sensitive errors and longer latencies on memory-guided saccades but not on visually guided saccades, indicating a selective role of D1 receptors in the mnemonic functions of prefrontal cortex (monkey).

In monkeys performing a spatial working memory task, low levels of D1 receptor stimulation enhanced the spatial tuning of prefrontal neurons by suppressing responses to nonpreferred directions, whereas high levels reduced delay-related firing for all directions and eroded tuning: an inverted U at the cellular level, mediated in monkeys and rats by cAMP signalling.
