In dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during a spatial working memory task, persistent firing of Delay cells was abolished by local blockade of NR2B-containing NMDA receptors or by systemic ketamine, while AMPA receptors contributed background depolarization; many Response cells were instead sensitive to AMPA receptor blockade and increased firing after ketamine (monkey).

Stimulating alpha2A adrenoceptors, inhibiting cAMP or blocking HCN channels enhanced the spatially tuned delay-related firing of prefrontal neurons, whereas excessive cAMP collapsed it; HCN channels and alpha2A adrenoceptors were colocalized in dendritic spines, and blocking or knocking down HCN1 channels in prefrontal cortex improved working memory (monkeys and rats).

Review: even mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities, and more prolonged stress causes architectural changes in prefrontal dendrites; the signalling pathways involved offer clues to why insults that disinhibit stress signalling can lead to symptoms of prefrontal dysfunction in mental illness.

In 175 patients with schizophrenia, 219 unaffected siblings and 55 controls, the low-activity Met allele of the COMT Val108/158 Met polymorphism predicted fewer perseverative errors on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test and a more efficient prefrontal response during working memory, and the Val allele was transmitted more often to offspring with schizophrenia. The authors suggest that the Val allele, by increasing prefrontal dopamine catabolism, impairs prefrontal cognition and slightly increases risk for schizophrenia (human).

Review: proposes that cognitive control stems from the active maintenance of patterns of activity in prefrontal cortex that represent goals and the means to achieve them, which provide bias signals guiding the flow of activity in other brain structures along the pathways a task needs.

In monkeys performing an object sequence memory task, prefrontal neurons with mixed selectivity encoded distributed information about all task-relevant aspects, giving high-dimensional representations with a computational advantage for readout; this dimensionality collapsed in error trials (monkey).

In monkeys trained to flexibly select and integrate noisy sensory inputs towards a choice, the complex responses of single prefrontal neurons were understood as part of population dynamics that a trained recurrent neural network reproduced, suggesting that selection and integration are two aspects of a single dynamical process within the same prefrontal circuits (monkey).

In prefrontal cortex during a working memory task, brief bursts of narrow-band gamma (45-100 Hz) accompanied encoding and re-activation of sensory information, while beta (20-35 Hz) bursts reflected a default state interrupted by encoding and decoding; this supports the hypothesis that working memory is manifested by discrete oscillatory dynamics and spiking, not sustained activity (monkey).

Monkeys learned two abstract rules (judge whether two successive pictures were the same or different, depending on which rule was in effect) and applied them to new pictures; the most prevalent neuronal activity in prefrontal cortex reflected the coding of these abstract rules (monkey).

During economic choice between goods, neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex encoded the value of offered and chosen goods independently of visuospatial factors and motor responses, so OFC neurons seem to be a good candidate network for the value assignment underlying economic choice (monkey).

Theory: proposes that the orbitofrontal cortex provides a labeling of the current task state, a cognitive map of task space used for reinforcement learning elsewhere in the brain, which is especially critical when task states include unobservable information; the framework is used to explain findings in reversal learning, delayed alternation, extinction and devaluation.

Excitotoxic, fiber-sparing lesions confined to the orbitofrontal cortex altered neither object reversal learning nor fear of snakes, and a previously reported loss of inhibitory control was traced to damage to nearby fiber tracts; the authors conclude that OFC has a more specialized role in reward-guided behavior and emotion than thought, including value updating (monkey).

Monkeys with bilateral orbital prefrontal removals showed attenuated reinforcer devaluation effects and were impaired on object reversal learning, but learned object discriminations and chose among foods normally, suggesting that orbital prefrontal cortex is critical for response selection based on predicted reward outcomes (monkey).

In the Stroop colour-naming task, controlling for repetition effects, conflict-related activity in the anterior cingulate cortex predicted both greater prefrontal cortex activity and adjustments in behaviour, supporting a role of ACC conflict monitoring in engaging cognitive control (human).

Humans alternated between comparative decision-making and foraging, which depended on distinct mechanisms in ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex: vmPFC encoded the values of specific well-defined options, whereas ACC encoded the average value of the foraging environment and the cost of foraging (human).

Theory: proposes that the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex allocates cognitive control according to its expected value, integrating the expected payoff of a controlled process, the amount of control it needs and the cost of cognitive effort to decide whether, where and how much control to allocate.

Infralimbic neurons fired to the tone only when rats were recalling extinction on the day after extinction training, and the rats that froze least showed the greatest increase in these responses; pairing conditioned tones with brief infralimbic stimulation lowered freezing in rats that had not been extinguished. The authors suggest that consolidation of extinction potentiates infralimbic activity, which inhibits fear (rat).

Inactivation with muscimol before extinction training showed dissociable roles: inactivating infralimbic cortex spared fear expression but impaired the acquisition and memory of extinction, inactivating prelimbic cortex impaired fear expression without affecting extinction memory, and inactivating the basolateral amygdala or ventral hippocampus impaired both (rat).

Prelimbic neurons showed sustained conditioned responses to a 30 s tone that correlated second by second with freezing, and their persistence after extinction training was associated with failure to express extinction memory; the authors suggest that prelimbic cortex transforms transient amygdala inputs into a sustained output that drives conditioned fear (rat).

Theta-range (4-12 Hz) synchrony between medial prefrontal cortex and basolateral amygdala increased only in mice that differentiated aversive from safe cues, and during recognized safety, in both learned fear and innate anxiety, BLA firing became entrained to theta input from mPFC, suggesting a safety-signalling mechanism by which mPFC diminishes fear (mouse).

Rats with prelimbic lesions were insensitive to changes in reward value after either limited or extended training, whereas rats with infralimbic lesions stayed sensitive to goal value even after extended training; this double dissociation suggests that prelimbic cortex supports goal-directed performance and infralimbic cortex lets extended training override it as habits form (rat).

Inhibiting parvalbumin interneurons optogenetically suppressed gamma oscillations in vivo, whereas driving them was sufficient to generate emergent gamma-frequency rhythmicity; gamma-frequency modulation of excitatory input enhanced signal transmission in neocortex by reducing circuit noise and amplifying circuit signals (mouse).

Optogenetically inhibiting somatostatin, but not parvalbumin, interneurons in medial prefrontal cortex during the encoding phase of a spatial working memory task impaired accuracy, with decreased hippocampal-prefrontal synchrony and impaired spatial encoding by mPFC neurons, suggesting that interneuron dysfunction may contribute to cognitive deficits in schizophrenia (mouse).

Direct hippocampal-prefrontal afferents were critical for encoding, but not maintenance or retrieval, of spatial cues in a working memory task; prefrontal units represented the cues in a hippocampal-input-dependent manner only during cue encoding, and successful encoding appeared to be mediated by gamma-frequency synchrony between the two structures (mouse).

Simultaneous tetrode recordings from hippocampal CA1 and medial prefrontal cortex showed that correlated firing between the two was selectively enhanced during behaviour that recruits spatial working memory, paralleled by enhanced coupling in the 4-12 Hz theta range (rat).

In mice using two rules to guide attention, mediodorsal thalamic input sustained rule representations in prefrontal cortex without relaying categorical information, by amplifying local PFC connectivity so that rule-specific neural sequences emerge; broadly enhancing PFC excitability diminished rule specificity and performance, whereas enhancing mediodorsal excitability improved both (mouse).

Pathway-specific inhibition showed directional interactions: mediodorsal thalamus-to-mPFC projections supported working memory maintenance and mPFC-to-MD projections supported the subsequent choice; mPFC neurons with elevated delay spiking, absent on error trials, required MD input for sustained maintenance, and enhancing MD excitability improved performance (mouse).

Many medial prefrontal neurons were modulated moment to moment by rats' decision to act in a challenging situation, yet activating mPFC principal neurons as a whole had no detectable effect; selectively activating mPFC cells projecting to the dorsal raphe nucleus induced a profound, rapid and reversible effect on selection of the active behavioural state (rat).

Dominance rank in mice was transitive and relatively stable; layer V pyramidal neurons of medial prefrontal cortex received stronger excitatory synaptic inputs in higher-ranking mice, and molecular manipulations that increased or decreased synaptic efficacy in dorsal mPFC neurons moved animals up or down the social rank (mouse).

Simultaneous recordings showed that prefrontal neurons reflected the target location first during top-down attention, whereas posterior parietal neurons signalled it earlier during bottom-up attention; frontal-parietal synchrony was stronger at lower frequencies during top-down and at higher frequencies during bottom-up attention (monkey).

Damage to lateral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann's area 9) caused a loss of inhibitory control in attentional selection, whereas damage to orbitofrontal cortex caused a loss of inhibitory control in affective processing, impairing the ability to alter behaviour when the emotional significance of stimuli changed (marmoset).

Ibotenic acid lesions of medial frontal cortex impaired neither initial acquisition nor reversal learning but selectively impaired shifting of attentional set, as in primates with prefrontal lesions; the authors conclude that rat medial frontal cortex has functional similarity to primate lateral prefrontal cortex (rat).

In 20 medication-free patients with chronic schizophrenia and 25 controls, blood flow to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex rose during the Wisconsin Card Sort in controls but not in patients, a regionally specific difference; in patients, DLPFC blood flow correlated positively with card-sort performance (human).

Dendritic spine density on deep layer 3 pyramidal neurons of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (area 46) was 23% lower in 15 subjects with schizophrenia than in normal controls, whereas superficial layer 3 neurons of area 46 and layer 3 neurons of primary visual cortex did not differ significantly: a region- and disease-specific decrease (human).

Review: convergent findings indicate that deficient TrkB signalling reduces GABA synthesis in parvalbumin-containing interneurons of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia, and the resulting alteration in perisomatic inhibition of pyramidal neurons contributes to a diminished capacity for the gamma-frequency synchronized activity required for working memory.

Chronic deep brain stimulation of white matter tracts adjacent to the subgenual cingulate gyrus (Brodmann area 25), a region metabolically overactive in treatment-resistant depression, was associated with striking and sustained remission in four of six patients, with reduced local blood flow and changes in downstream limbic and cortical sites (human).

Ketamine rapidly activated the mTOR pathway, increasing synaptic signalling proteins and the number and function of new spine synapses in prefrontal cortex; blocking mTOR signalling completely blocked ketamine's induction of synaptogenesis and its behavioural responses in models of depression (rat).

Longitudinal imaging of medial prefrontal microcircuits showed that depression-related behaviour was associated with branch-specific elimination of dendritic spines on prefrontal projection neurons; antidepressant-dose ketamine selectively rescued eliminated spines and restored coordinated ensemble activity, and this spinogenesis was required for long-term maintenance, but not initial induction, of ketamine's effects on motivated escape behaviour (mouse).

In 824 MRI scans from 223 children with ADHD and 223 typically developing controls, the age of peak cortical thickness was delayed in ADHD throughout most of the cerebrum (median 10.5 versus 7.5 years), most prominently in prefrontal regions important for control of cognitive processes including attention and motor planning (human).

Damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex causes a defect in real-life decision-making; on a new task simulating such decisions under uncertainty, with reward and punishment, prefrontal patients, unlike controls, were oblivious to the future consequences of their actions and seemed guided by immediate prospects only (human).

Six patients with focal bilateral damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex gave abnormally 'utilitarian' judgements on moral dilemmas that pit aggregate welfare against highly emotionally aversive actions, but normal judgements on other classes of dilemmas, indicating that for this selective set the VMPC is critical for normal judgements of right and wrong (human).

Review: a meta-analysis found dramatic differences in the focus of human and rodent PFC research, leading rodent atlases use inconsistent anatomical terms and criteria for PFC areas, and a survey of PFC researchers found little consensus; the authors propose an alternative scheme for interpreting rodent data based on the corpus callosum and primate anterior cingulate nomenclature.

A type of midbrain dopamine neuron with unconventional fast-firing properties and small DAT/TH mRNA ratios projects selectively to prefrontal cortex, the nucleus accumbens core and medial shell and the basolateral amygdala, whereas conventional slow-firing dopamine neurons project only to the lateral accumbens shell and dorsolateral striatum; only the mesoprefrontal neurons lack functional somatodendritic Girk2-coupled D2 autoreceptors (mouse).

Locus coeruleus cells innervating different cortical regions were biochemically and electrophysiologically distinct, eliciting greater release of norepinephrine in prefrontal than in motor cortex, which challenges the view of the LC as a relatively homogeneous modulator of forebrain activity (rat).

Optogenetically evoked dopamine release from VTA projections in medial prefrontal cortex was neither rewarding nor aversive, but repeatedly pairing it with an auditory stimulus sped later learning to discriminate that stimulus, with appetitive or aversive outcomes alike; the pairings increased mPFC responses to the stimulus, and D1 or D2 antagonists in mPFC impaired discrimination. The authors conclude that dopamine transients tune mPFC neurons for recognizing behaviourally relevant events during learning (mouse).

WGA-HRP injections into the mediodorsal nucleus labeled cells and terminals in prefrontal cortex in a nucleus-to-field pattern: the magnocellular part with ventral and medial prefrontal areas (11-14), the parvicellular part with dorsolateral and dorsomedial areas (46, 9 and 8B); MD terminals were confined to layer IV and adjacent deep layer III (monkey).

Retrograde tracing in 27 monkeys showed that most hippocampal-formation neurons projecting to prefrontal cortex target medial areas, followed by orbital areas, whereas lateral prefrontal areas receive only a few, mostly subicular, neurons and their most robust input from the presubiculum and area 29a-c (monkey).

Tracers injected in the amygdala showed that prefrontal areas vary vastly in their connections with it, densest in posterior orbitofrontal and posterior medial cortices and sparsest in anterior lateral areas, especially area 10; cingulate areas 25 and 24 sent comparatively more projections to the amygdala than they received, whereas caudal orbitofrontal areas were more receivers than senders (monkey).

In rats with 6-OHDA lesions of the nigrostriatal dopamine pathway (a Parkinson's disease model), striatopallidal neurons raise their mRNAs for the D2 receptor and enkephalin, and striatonigral neurons lower theirs for the D1 receptor and substance P; the D2 agonist quinpirole and the D1 agonist SKF-38393 reverse these changes, so dopamine's differential effects on the two striatal output systems are mediated by D1 receptors (striatonigral) and D2 receptors (striatopallidal).

Review: proposes a model in which specific basal ganglia disorders reflect changed function of subpopulations of striatal projection neurons: hyperkinetic disorders are postulated to result from selective impairment of striatal neurons projecting to the lateral globus pallidus, and hypokinetic disorders such as Parkinson's disease are hypothesized to result from changes in these subpopulations that increase basal ganglia output.

Review: both hypokinetic (Parkinson's disease) and hyperkinetic (Huntington's disease, hemiballismus) movement disorders can be accounted for by postulating specific disturbances within the basal ganglia–thalamocortical 'motor' circuit; describes the changes in its neuronal activity in primate models of these disorders.

Bilateral optogenetic excitation of indirect-pathway medium spiny neurons elicited a parkinsonian state (more freezing, bradykinesia, fewer locomotor initiations), whereas activating direct-pathway neurons reduced freezing and increased locomotion, and in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease completely rescued deficits in freezing, bradykinesia and locomotor initiation.

Both direct- and indirect-pathway spiny projection neurons in dorsal striatum showed transient increases in activity when mice initiated actions, but not when they were inactive; concurrent activation of both pathways in one hemisphere preceded contraversive movements and predicted specific movements within 500 ms, challenging the classical view of opposing pathways (mouse).

Both the direct striatonigral and the indirect striatopallidal pathways are necessary for smooth initiation and execution of learned action sequences: inhibiting or stimulating either before initiation increased its latency (striatonigral manipulations slowed initiation, striatopallidal ones aborted it), and inhibiting either after initiation impaired execution, suggesting a supportive versus permissive model (mouse).

Review: dopaminergic neurons in the primate have a fluctuating output that apparently signals changes or errors in the predictions of future salient and rewarding events, findings that can be understood through quantitative theories of adaptive optimizing control.

Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons concurrent with reward delivery, mimicking a prediction error, was sufficient to cause long-lasting increases in cue-elicited reward seeking in blocking and extinction procedures, establishing a causal role for temporally precise dopamine neuron signaling in cue–reward learning (rat).

Stimulating the substantia nigra with the parameters optimal for lever pressing in intracranial self-stimulation induced potentiation of corticostriatal synapses that required dopamine receptor activation; the degree of potentiation within ten minutes correlated with the time the rats took to learn the task, and the authors propose that this potentiation reinforces the learned behaviour (rat).

In brain slices from dopamine-receptor transgenic mice, plasticity at cortical synapses onto D1 and D2 medium spiny neurons was not unidirectional in each cell type as postulated: dopamine plays complementary roles in the two types that make synaptic plasticity bidirectional and Hebbian, and in models of Parkinson's disease this balance is lost, giving unidirectional changes that could underlie network pathology and symptoms.

In monkeys made parkinsonian with MPTP, lesions of the subthalamic nucleus reduced all major motor disturbances in the contralateral limbs, including akinesia, rigidity and tremor, supporting the postulated role of excessive subthalamic activity in Parkinson's disease.

In 24 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease given bilateral subthalamic stimulation (20 followed for at least 12 months), off-medication activities of daily living and motor scores (Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale parts II and III) improved by 60 percent after one year, on-medication motor scores by 10 percent, and the dopaminergic dose was halved; cognitive scores were unchanged, and one patient had paralysis and aphasia after an intracerebral hematoma at implantation.

In a randomized trial of 255 patients with advanced Parkinson disease, bilateral deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus gave a mean 4.6 h/d more on time without troubling dyskinesia at 6 months, versus 0 h/d with best medical therapy, and improved motor function and quality of life, with small decrements in some areas of information processing and more serious adverse events (49 versus 15 patients).

In a 2-year randomized trial of 251 patients with Parkinson's disease and early motor complications, subthalamic stimulation plus medical therapy was superior to medical therapy alone for quality of life (a between-group difference of 8.0 points on the PDQ-39), motor disability, activities of daily living, levodopa-induced motor complications and time with good mobility and no dyskinesia; serious adverse events occurred in 54.8 percent versus 44.1 percent of patients.

Optogenetically driving or inhibiting distinct circuit elements in freely moving parkinsonian rodents showed that therapeutic effects within the subthalamic nucleus can be accounted for by direct selective stimulation of afferent axons projecting to this region, giving insight into the mechanisms of deep brain stimulation.

In Parkinsonian rats, the external globus pallidus has two GABAergic populations: prototypic neurons fire antiphase to subthalamic neurons, often express parvalbumin and target downstream basal ganglia nuclei including the subthalamic nucleus, whereas arkypallidal neurons fire in phase with it, express preproenkephalin and innervate only the striatum, providing its largest extrinsic GABAergic innervation.

In rats performing a Stop task, arkypallidal globus pallidus neurons had earlier and stronger Stop responses than prototypical ones, selective to Stop rather than Go cues and timed with the suppression of developing striatal Go-related activity, supporting a two-step model of action suppression: a pause via a subthalamic-nigral pathway, then cancellation via arkypallidal GABAergic projections to striatum.

Review: the cortico-subthalamo-pallidal 'hyperdirect' pathway conveys powerful excitation from motor-related cortical areas to the globus pallidus, bypassing the striatum with a shorter conduction time; the authors propose a center–surround model in which a hyperdirect signal first inhibits broad areas of thalamus and cortex, the direct pathway then releases only the selected motor program, and the indirect pathway possibly inhibits the targets extensively afterwards.

After training under interval schedules, which generate habits, rats with dorsolateral striatum lesions, unlike sham-operated and dorsomedial-lesioned rats, reduced lever pressing when the outcome was devalued, showing that the dorsolateral striatum is necessary for habit formation and suggesting that control then reverts to the goal-directed system.

Optical recordings revealed rapid phasic signalling in striatum-targeting dopaminergic axons that was associated with, and capable of triggering, locomotion; these axons were largely distinct from those that responded to unexpected rewards (mouse).

A large proportion of SNc dopamine neurons, not overlapping with reward-responsive ones, transiently increased their activity before self-paced movement initiation, related to the vigour of future movements; inhibiting them while mice were immobile reduced, and brief activation increased, the probability and vigour of future movements, whereas manipulations after initiation did not affect ongoing movements (mouse).

Distinct classes of dorsal striatal neurons represent movement vigor; mice with progressive depletion of midbrain dopamine neurons showed a progressive reduction in vigor and a selective impairment of its striatal representation, both ameliorated by restoring dopaminergic tone with a synthetic precursor, and suppressing striatal activity during movement was sufficient to reduce vigor (mouse).

A new gene on 4p16.3, IT15, contains a polymorphic (CAG)n trinucleotide repeat that is expanded and unstable on Huntington's disease chromosomes, longer than the normal range in all 75 disease families examined; the repeat appears to lie within the coding sequence of a widely expressed protein of about 348 kd.

In 17 Huntington disease specimens, enkephalin-containing striatal neurons projecting to the external globus pallidus were much more affected in early and middle stages than substance P-containing neurons projecting to the internal pallidal segment, and substance P neurons projecting to the substantia nigra pars reticulata more than those projecting to the pars compacta; at the most advanced stages all striatal projections were depleted, except for some apparent sparing of the projection to the pars compacta.

A mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene, which codes for a presynaptic protein thought to be involved in neuronal plasticity, was identified in an Italian kindred and in three unrelated families of Greek origin with autosomal dominant inheritance of Parkinson's disease.

Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites from Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies stain strongly for alpha-synuclein, which labels more structures than ubiquitin, and filaments extracted from Lewy bodies are labelled by anti-alpha-synuclein antibodies, indicating that alpha-synuclein forms their major filamentous component.

Four people developed marked parkinsonism after intravenous use of an illicit drug; the substance two of them injected was primarily MPTP, and from their features and the pathology of one earlier case the authors propose that this chemical selectively damages cells in the substantia nigra.

In a 40-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 361 patients with early Parkinson's disease, followed by 2 weeks off treatment, parkinsonism worsened more with placebo than with any levodopa dose, yet striatal dopamine-transporter uptake declined more with levodopa; the authors conclude that levodopa either slows progression or has a prolonged effect on symptoms, and that its long-term effects remain uncertain.

In local potentials recorded from the internal globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus of four patients after surgery for Parkinson's disease, power within and coherence between the nuclei were dominated by activity below 30 Hz off medication; levodopa reduced this low-frequency activity and brought a new peak at about 70 Hz, so the pattern of synchronization depends critically on dopaminergic activity.

Injecting the GABA agonist muscimol into the substantia nigra pars reticulata made monkeys produce irrepressible saccades toward the contralateral field, most disrupting saccades to remembered targets, as bicuculline in the superior colliculus does; the authors conclude that the pars reticulata exerts a tonic GABA-mediated inhibition on saccade-related collicular cells, and suggest that the basal ganglia contribute to initiating movement by releasing the target structure from tonic inhibition.

As mice learned a self-paced action sequence, neural activity in nigrostriatal circuits came to signal specifically the initiation or termination of each sequence, not interval timing, movement speed or action value; genetically altering striatal circuit function disrupted the development of this start/stop activity and selectively impaired sequence learning.

Across retrograde and anterograde tracing experiments, striatonigrostriatal projections form an ascending spiral through midbrain dopamine cells: the ventromedial (limbic) striatum projects to a wide range of dopamine cells but receives a relatively small dopamine input, the dorsolateral striatum receives input from a broad expanse of them, and the shell influences the core, the core the central striatum, and the central striatum the dorsolateral striatum (monkey).

In 8 patients with advanced Parkinson disease, subthalamic stimulation delivered only when a brain–computer interface detected pathological activity in local field potentials from the stimulation electrodes (adaptive DBS) improved motor scores by 66 percent unblinded and 50 percent blinded, 29 and 27 percent more than conventional continuous stimulation, with 56 percent less stimulation time.
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): reports loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions (human).

Patient R.B. developed marked anterograde amnesia, little if any retrograde amnesia and no other cognitive impairment after an ischemic episode; histology found a circumscribed bilateral lesion of the entire CA1 field, the only damage that could reasonably be associated with the memory defect (human).

Review: studies of human amnesia and of a monkey model identify a medial temporal lobe memory system, the hippocampus with entorhinal, perirhinal and parahippocampal cortices, that is essential for establishing long-term memory for facts and events (declarative memory) and binds together distributed neocortical storage sites; its role is temporary, as memory gradually becomes independent of it.

Amnesic patients with primary bilateral hippocampal damage were markedly impaired at imagining new experiences from short verbal cues; their imagined scenes were fragmented and lacked spatial coherence, suggesting the hippocampus may provide the spatial context that binds the elements of an experience (human).

Review: memories of everyday life depend initially on the medial temporal lobe system, including the hippocampus, and are thought to become increasingly dependent on cortex as they mature; reviews how remote memories are organized in the cortex and the molecular and cellular events of their consolidation.

In a hippocampal-dependent flavor-place paired-associate task, memory became persistent as a putative neocortical schema developed; new associations trained in one trial were then assimilated and rapidly became hippocampal-independent, so systems consolidation can be extremely quick when a schema exists (rat).

Prefrontal engram cells critical for remote contextual fear memory were generated during initial learning through inputs from the hippocampal-entorhinal network and the basolateral amygdala, and matured with time with support from hippocampal engram cells; hippocampal engram cells gradually became silent, whereas basolateral amygdala engram cells, necessary for the fear memory, were maintained (mouse).

Licensed London taxi drivers had larger posterior hippocampi than controls, and a more anterior hippocampal region was larger in controls; hippocampal volume correlated with time spent as a taxi driver, positively in the posterior and negatively in the anterior hippocampus (human).

Recordings from 317 neurons in the medial temporal and frontal lobes of subjects navigating a virtual town found cells that respond at specific spatial locations, present primarily in the hippocampus, and cells that respond to views of landmarks, mainly in the parahippocampal region (human).

High-resolution fMRI during incidental encoding found activity with a strong bias toward pattern separation in, and limited to, the CA3/dentate gyrus, whereas CA1, the subiculum and the entorhinal and parahippocampal cortices showed activity consistent with a bias toward pattern completion (human).
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): presents preliminary evidence from unit activity in the freely moving rat that the hippocampus acts as a spatial map.
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): place navigation is impaired in rats with hippocampal lesions.

Place cells that fired together when the animal occupied particular locations showed an increased tendency to fire together during subsequent slow-wave sleep, compared with sleep before the task, an effect that declined gradually during each post-behavior sleep session (rat).

As a rat traverses a place field, the theta phase at which a place cell fires shifts systematically, moving progressively forward on each theta cycle (a precession of 100 to 355 degrees in different cells), and the phase correlates more with spatial location than with time since entering the field (rat).

The dorsocaudal medial entorhinal cortex contains grid cells, activated whenever the animal's position coincides with a vertex of a regular grid of equilateral triangles; neighbouring cells share orientation and spacing but differ in phase, spacing increases from dorsal to ventral, and the map is anchored to landmarks but persists without them, suggesting a path-integration-based map (rat).

Layer II of the medial entorhinal cortex was predominated by grid cells, whereas in deeper layers grid cells colocalized with head-direction cells and conjunctive grid × head-direction cells, and all cell types were modulated by running speed (rat).

Inactivating the medial septum with muscimol reduced theta rhythm, and medial entorhinal grid cells lost their spatial periodicity while head-direction cells maintained their selectivity, supporting the hypothesis that spatial coding by grid cells requires theta oscillations (rat).

Grid-like firing in the entorhinal cortex vanished when intraseptal lidocaine reduced theta oscillations, whereas other spatially modulated entorhinal cells and hippocampal place cells retained their spatial firing patterns to a larger extent (rat).

Recordings from neurosurgical patients performing a virtual-navigation task identified cells with grid-like spiking patterns in the human brain, suggesting that humans and simpler animals rely on homologous spatial-coding schemes (human).

Hippocampal 'time cells' encoded successive moments during an empty gap between key events while also encoding location and ongoing behavior, and most formed different representations ('retimed') when the main temporal parameter was altered, much as place cells remap (rat).

Before goal-directed navigation in an open arena, the hippocampus generated brief place-cell sequences encoding trajectories biased to progress from the current location to a known goal; the sequences predicted immediate future behavior, even for novel combinations of start and goal (rat).

In anaesthetized rabbits, conditioning trains to the perforant path potentiated the population response of dentate granule cells for 30 min to 10 hr in 15 of 18 animals, suggested to reflect both increased efficiency of perforant path synaptic transmission and increased excitability of the granule cells (rabbit).

Chronic intraventricular infusion of the NMDA receptor antagonist D,L-AP5 selectively impaired place learning, which is sensitive to hippocampal damage, but not visual discrimination learning, and suppressed hippocampal LTP in vivo; the L-isomer had no behavioral effect (rat).

Mice with deletion of the NMDAR1 gene restricted to CA1 pyramidal cells lacked NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents and long-term potentiation at CA1 synapses and had impaired spatial memory but unimpaired nonspatial learning (mouse).

One-trial inhibitory avoidance learning produced the same changes in hippocampal glutamate receptors as LTP induced by high-frequency stimulation, caused a spatially restricted increase in evoked synaptic transmission in CA1 in vivo, and occluded stimulation-induced LTP, so the training induces LTP in CA1 (rat).

Mice with the NMDA receptor gene ablated specifically in adult CA3 pyramidal cells acquired and retrieved spatial reference memory in the Morris water maze normally but were impaired at retrieving it from a fraction of the original cues, and their CA1 place-related activity fell upon partial cue removal (mouse).
Selectively eliminating sharp wave-ripple complexes during post-training consolidation periods impaired performance on a hippocampus-dependent spatial memory task (rat).

Stimulating hippocampal afferents to disrupt neuronal activity during ripple events in the 1-hour rest after one of two spatial navigation tasks, without changing sleep-wake structure, made rats learn that task more slowly than the control task (rat).

Review: sharp wave-ripples, the most synchronous population pattern in the mammalian brain, occur during 'off-line' states, arise from the excitatory recurrent system of CA3 and drive a fast ripple oscillation in CA1; they replay fragments of waking sequences in compressed form, assist memory consolidation (selective disruption interferes with memory) and may influence decisions and planning, and their pathological conversion ('p-ripples') marks epileptogenic tissue.

Minimal changes in the shape of the environment substantially altered correlated activity patterns among place-modulated dentate gyrus granule cells, whereas more different environments recruited new cell populations in CA3 but not in the dentate gyrus, implying a dual mechanism for pattern separation (rat).

Mice lacking the NMDA receptor subunit NR1 specifically in dentate gyrus granule cells performed normally in contextual fear conditioning but were impaired at distinguishing two similar contexts, and their CA3 pyramidal cells showed less context-specific modulation of firing rate (mouse).

In postmortem tissue from patients treated with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU), new neurons, identified with BrdU and NeuN, calbindin or neuron-specific enolase, were generated from dividing progenitor cells in the dentate gyrus of adult humans, indicating that the human hippocampus retains the ability to generate neurons throughout life (human).

Proliferating progenitors and young neurons in the human dentate gyrus declined sharply during the first year of life, only a few isolated young neurons were seen at 7 and 13 years, and none were detected in adults (17 post-mortem controls, 12 epilepsy resections); in macaques, neurogenesis decreased during juvenile development, so dentate neurogenesis does not continue, or is extremely rare, in adult humans (human, monkey).

Whole autopsy hippocampi from healthy individuals aged 14 to 79 had similar numbers of intermediate neural progenitors and thousands of immature neurons in the dentate gyrus across ages, although older individuals had less angiogenesis and neuroplasticity and a smaller quiescent progenitor pool in the anterior-mid dentate gyrus (human).

Disrupting antidepressant-induced neurogenesis blocked behavioral responses to antidepressants: serotonin 1A receptor null mice were insensitive to the neurogenic and behavioral effects of fluoxetine, and X-irradiating a restricted region containing the hippocampus prevented the neurogenic and behavioral effects of two classes of antidepressants (mouse).

Adult mice with ablated hippocampal neurogenesis were impaired at spatial discrimination in a radial arm maze and a touch-screen task when stimuli were presented with little spatial separation, but not when they were widely separated, suggesting that newborn neurons may be necessary for normal pattern separation (mouse).

methods: inducible genetic expansion of adult-born neurons
finding: Inducibly increasing the survival of adult-born dentate neurons made mice more efficient at differentiating overlapping contextual representations (enhanced pattern separation), with normal object recognition, spatial learning, contextual fear conditioning and extinction; increasing neurogenesis alone did not produce a response like that of anxiolytics or antidepressants (mouse).

Optogenetically reactivating dentate gyrus neurons labelled with channelrhodopsin-2 during fear conditioning induced freezing in a different context, which did not occur in non-conditioned mice, with enhanced yellow fluorescent protein instead of channelrhodopsin-2, or with cells labelled in a context not associated with fear, so activating a sparse engram ensemble is sufficient for recall of that memory (mouse).

Optogenetically reactivating dentate gyrus neurons labelled during exposure to one context while mice were fear-conditioned in another made them freeze in the first context, where no shock was ever delivered; this false memory was context-specific and activated downstream regions similar to those engaged by natural fear memory recall (mouse).

Hippocampal lesions made 1 day after fear conditioning abolished contextual fear, whereas rats lesioned after longer intervals (lesions were made 1, 7, 14 or 28 days after training) retained significant contextual fear, and fear of the tone was unaffected at any interval, suggesting a time-limited hippocampal role in contextual fear memory (rat).

Amygdala lesions interfered with fear conditioning to both a tone and the context, whereas hippocampal lesions interfered with conditioning to the context but not to the tone, suggesting an associative role for the amygdala and a sensory relay role for the hippocampus in fear conditioning (rat).

In 83 autopsy brains, amyloid deposits were of limited use for staging, whereas neurofibrillary tangles and neuropil threads followed a characteristic distribution defining six stages: transentorhinal (I-II), limbic (III-IV, with the entorhinal cortex proper and mild involvement of the first Ammon's horn sector) and isocortical (V-VI, with destruction of virtually all isocortical association areas) (human).

In Alzheimer patients, pathology specifically affected cells of the subiculum and of layers II and IV of the entorhinal cortex, the cells that interconnect the hippocampal formation with the association cortices, basal forebrain, thalamus and hypothalamus; this pattern isolates the hippocampal formation from much of its input and output and probably contributes to the memory disorder (human).

Stereological counts showed that people with very mild Alzheimer's disease (CDR 0.5) had 32% fewer entorhinal neurons than cognitively normal controls, with 60% fewer in layer II and 40% fewer in layer IV, and about 90% and 70% fewer in severe dementia; neuron number was inversely proportional to neurofibrillary tangles and neuritic plaques (human).

Subjects with a history of major depressive episodes, in remission, had significantly smaller left and right hippocampal volumes than matched controls, with no difference in total cerebral volume, and the reduction correlated with the total duration of major depression (human).

In monozygotic twins discordant for trauma exposure, PTSD severity in exposed patients correlated negatively with the hippocampal volume of both the patients and their trauma-unexposed co-twins, and severe-PTSD twin pairs had smaller hippocampi than non-PTSD pairs, evidence that smaller hippocampi are a risk factor for stress-related psychopathology (human).

Review: behavioral, anatomical and gene expression studies support three hippocampal compartments; the dorsal hippocampus (posterior in primates) performs primarily cognitive functions, and the ventral (anterior in primates) relates to stress, emotion and affect, with gene expression correlating with the amygdala and hypothalamus.

Review: the dominant 'dichotomy view', with the dorsal (posterior) hippocampus implicated in memory and navigation and the ventral (anterior) in anxiety-related behaviours, may need revision; gene expression shows sharply demarcated domains along the long axis, whereas anatomy and rodent recordings suggest gradients, leading to a model of gradients superimposed on discrete domains.

Optogenetically elevating or decreasing granule-cell activity showed that cells in the dorsal dentate gyrus control exploratory drive and the encoding, not retrieval, of contextual fear memories, whereas elevating activity in the ventral dentate gyrus had no effect on contextual learning but powerfully suppressed innate anxiety (mouse).

Subsets of ventral CA1 neurons changed firing at places of elevated anxiety or during goal approach; anxiety-related firing was selectively increased in neurons projecting to the prefrontal cortex, goal-directed firing was most prominent in neurons targeting the nucleus accumbens, and triple-projecting neurons (prefrontal cortex, amygdala and nucleus accumbens) were most active during tasks and sharp wave/ripples (rat).

Optogenetically inhibiting ventral hippocampal input to the medial prefrontal cortex disrupted anxiety-related behavior and prefrontal representations of aversion and reduced theta synchrony in a pathway-, frequency- and task-specific manner; bilateral, but not unilateral, inhibition also altered physiological correlates of anxiety in the basolateral amygdala (mouse).

Dorsal CA1 was enriched in place cells and ventral CA1 in anxiety cells, activated by anxiogenic environments and required for avoidance, which were enriched among neurons projecting to the lateral hypothalamic area rather than the basal amygdala; activating ventral CA1 terminals in the lateral hypothalamus, but not the basal amygdala, increased anxiety and avoidance, whereas activating terminals in the basal amygdala, but not the hypothalamus, impaired contextual fear memory (mouse).

Genetically targeted inactivation of CA2 pyramidal neurons in adult mice caused a pronounced loss of social memory, the ability to remember a conspecific, with no change in sociability or in several other hippocampus-dependent behaviors, including spatial and contextual memory (mouse).

Lesions of the lateral amygdaloid nucleus, a major subcortical target of the acoustic thalamus, but not of the striatum above it or the adjacent cortex, interfered with emotional conditioning to an auditory stimulus without affecting responses after random (nonassociative) training, so the lateral nucleus may be the sensory interface of the amygdala in emotional learning (rat).

Destroying either the thalamo-amygdala or the thalamo-cortico-amygdala auditory pathway alone had no effect on auditory fear conditioning (arterial pressure and freezing), but combined lesions of both pathways disrupted it (rat).

Lesions of the lateral hypothalamic area, a target of the central amygdaloid nucleus, interfered with the conditioned arterial pressure response but not conditioned freezing, whereas lesions of the caudal midbrain central gray disrupted freezing but not the pressure response, and lesions of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis affected neither, so different efferent projections of the central amygdala appear to mediate the autonomic and behavioral responses of conditioned fear (rat).

Fear conditioning itself produced a long-lasting increase in synaptic efficacy in the pathway from the medial geniculate nucleus to the lateral amygdala, measured in vitro as a presynaptic facilitation of AMPA-receptor-mediated transmission onto lateral amygdala neurons (rat).

Fear conditioning drove AMPA-type glutamate receptors into the synapses of a large fraction of lateral amygdala neurons, and blocking this synaptic incorporation in as few as 10 to 20% of lateral amygdala neurons reduced the memory (rat).

After rats learned to associate foot shock with optogenetic stimulation of auditory inputs to the amygdala, optogenetic long-term depression of those inputs inactivated the memory and subsequent optogenetic long-term potentiation reactivated it, supporting a causal link between these synaptic processes and memory (rat).

Changing CREB function in subsets of lateral amygdala neurons changed the probability that individual neurons were recruited into a fear memory trace, suggesting that eligible neurons compete and are selected according to their relative CREB activity at the time of learning (mouse).

Selectively deleting lateral amygdala neurons that overexpressed CREB after learning, but not a similar portion of random lateral amygdala neurons, blocked expression of that fear memory robustly and persistently, suggesting that the memory was permanently erased (mouse).

Infusing the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin into the lateral and basal amygdala shortly after a consolidated fear memory was reactivated, 1 or 14 days after conditioning, produced amnesia on later tests, whereas the same infusion without reactivation, or 6 hours after it, did not, so reactivated fear memories return to a labile state that requires protein synthesis for reconsolidation (rat).

Pairing a tone with optogenetic activation of lateral amygdala pyramidal neurons, instead of an aversive stimulus, made the tone alone produce behavioral fear responses, supporting the idea that fear learning is instructed by activation of these cells by aversive stimuli (rat).

In freely moving rats, fear conditioning increased tone-elicited responses of lateral amygdala neurons, often within the first few trials, made unresponsive cells tone-responsive and altered couplings between them, with the greatest effects on the shortest-latency (under 15 ms) components, consistent with direct projections from the auditory thalamus (rat).

Functional inactivation showed that the central nucleus of the amygdala is needed for the acquisition as well as the expression of fear conditioning, and inhibiting protein synthesis there after training impaired consolidation of the fear memory (rat).

Neuronal activity in the lateral subdivision of the central amygdala (CEl) was required for fear acquisition, whereas conditioned fear responses were driven by output neurons of the medial subdivision (CEm); cell-type-specific plasticity in the inhibitory CEl-to-CEm pathway may gate fear expression and regulate fear generalization (mouse).

PKC-δ+ GABAergic neurons in the lateral central amygdala inhibit output neurons of the medial central amygdala and make reciprocal inhibitory synapses with PKC-δ− neurons; silencing them suggests that they are the CEl "off" units inhibited by the conditioned stimulus, defining an inhibitory microcircuit that gates central amygdala output to control conditioned freezing (mouse).

Fear conditioning induced cell-specific, bidirectional, presynaptically expressed plasticity of lateral amygdala inputs onto inhibitory neurons of the lateral central amygdala; preventing potentiation onto somatostatin-positive neurons impaired fear memory formation, and activating these neurons was necessary for fear memory recall and sufficient to drive fear responses (mouse).

In mice that switch between conditioned freezing and flight, CRF+ central amygdala neurons mediated conditioned flight and activating SOM+ neurons initiated freezing; local inhibitory connections between the two populations regulate the balance, so competition between them selects the response (mouse).

An inhibitory pathway from the central amygdala to the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey produces freezing by disinhibiting ventrolateral periaqueductal grey excitatory outputs to premotor targets in the magnocellular nucleus of the medulla, and this freezing pathway interacts with circuits mediating flight (mouse).

Central amygdala projections to nuclei that modulate freezing or cardiovascular responses arose from separate neuronal populations that responded differently to oxytocin, and in vivo oxytocin decreased freezing in fear-conditioned rats without affecting the cardiovascular response (rat).

Axons of hypothalamic oxytocin neurons reach most forebrain regions, including the central amygdala, where optogenetically evoked oxytocin release activated a local GABAergic circuit that inhibited output neurons in vitro and robustly decreased freezing in fear-conditioned rats (rat).

PKC-δ+ neurons in the lateral central amygdala were activated by diverse anorexigenic signals, were required for those signals to inhibit feeding, and strongly suppressed food intake when activated (mouse).

Rhesus monkeys with bilateral excitotoxic lesions of the central nucleus of the amygdala showed less fear-related behavior toward a snake and less freezing toward a human intruder, lower cerebrospinal fluid CRF and lower plasma ACTH, but no change in asymmetric frontal EEG activity (monkey).

Transitions between high fear (context-dependent renewal) and low fear (extinction) were triggered by a rapid switch in the balance of activity between two distinct populations of basal amygdala neurons, differentially connected with the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex; reversibly inactivating the basal amygdala prevented these behavioral changes without affecting memory or behavioral expression (mouse).

Intercalated cells, which receive conditioned-stimulus information from the basolateral amygdala and send inhibitory projections to the central nucleus, were partly lesioned (34% fewer) with a toxin targeting μ-opioid-receptor-expressing cells; the lesions caused a marked deficit in the expression of fear extinction, larger the fewer intercalated neurons survived (rat).

Optogenetically stimulating basolateral amygdala terminals in the central amygdala acutely and reversibly reduced anxiety-related behaviors, and inhibiting the same projection increased them; these effects were not seen with direct optogenetic control of basolateral amygdala cell bodies (mouse).

Activating basolateral amygdala synapses in the ventral hippocampus acutely increased anxiety-related behaviors and inhibiting them decreased these behaviors; the inputs are monosynaptic and glutamatergic onto ventral hippocampal pyramidal neurons, with polysynaptic inhibition through local interneurons (mouse).

Basolateral amygdala neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens or to the centromedial amygdala underwent opposing synaptic changes after fear or reward conditioning; photostimulating the accumbens projectors supported positive reinforcement and the centromedial projectors negative reinforcement, and inhibiting the centromedial projectors impaired fear conditioning and enhanced reward conditioning (mouse).

Two genetically distinct, spatially segregated populations of excitatory basolateral amygdala neurons take part in negative- and positive-valence behaviors and are connected through mutual inhibition (mouse).

Mice worked to earn optical stimulation of basolateral amygdala glutamatergic inputs to the nucleus accumbens, an effect that required accumbal D1-type but not D2-type dopamine receptor signaling, and brief inhibition of these inputs reduced cue-evoked sucrose intake; stimulating medial prefrontal inputs to the accumbens did not support self-stimulation (mouse).

As abstract images acquired positive or negative value through conditioning and the values were then reversed, the activity of amygdala neurons was modulated by image value rapidly enough to account for, and correlated with, the monkeys' learning, and distinct populations encoded positive and negative values (monkey).

With competing shock- and sucrose-predictive cues, correlated firing between basolateral amygdala and prelimbic cortex was directed mainly from amygdala to prelimbic cortex during the shock cue, prelimbic-projecting amygdala neurons predicted behavior better than other amygdala neurons, and stimulating this projection increased freezing while inhibiting it reduced freezing (rat).

Review: although most views of the amygdala emphasize negative emotions such as fear, evidence supports a role in processing positive emotions as well, including learning about the beneficial biological value of stimuli, and its role in stimulus-reward learning might be as important as its role in fear conditioning.

Review: animal studies indicate that the basolateral amygdala mediates the memory-modulating effects of adrenal stress hormones and several classes of neurotransmitters, converging on noradrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic activation, and modulates consolidation of many kinds of memory through efferents to the caudate nucleus, nucleus accumbens and cortex; in human imaging, amygdala activation by emotional arousal during encoding correlates highly with later recall.

A rare patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage was impaired at recognizing fear in facial expressions and at recognizing multiple emotions in a single expression, but recognized personal identity from faces (human).

Patient SM's impaired recognition of fear stems from not making normal use of the eye region of faces, traced to a lack of spontaneous fixations on the eyes; her recognition of fearful faces became normal when she was instructed to look at the eyes (human).

Patient SM, who has focal bilateral amygdala lesions, showed no fear when exposed to live snakes and spiders, a haunted house or emotionally evocative films, and questionnaires and 3 months of experience sampling showed an impoverished experience of fear, although she exhibited other basic emotions (human).

A patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage did not acquire conditioned autonomic responses but learned the declarative facts about the stimulus pairings, a patient with selective bilateral hippocampal damage showed the reverse, and a patient with damage to both acquired neither (human).

People with unilateral temporal lobectomy showed impaired acquisition of conditioned fear responses on simple and conditional discrimination tasks, which could not be explained by sensory or autonomic deficits or by declarative memory for the task (human).
In PET, the left amygdala responded more to fearful than to happy faces, and its response increased with increasing fearfulness and decreased with increasing happiness (human).

Although most subjects reported seeing only neutral faces, fMRI signal in the amygdala was higher during backward-masked fearful than masked happy faces, with increases to fearful and decreases to happy faces (human).

Two people with focal bilateral amygdala lesions responded normally to changes in the expected value and risk of monetary gambles but showed a dramatic reduction in loss aversion compared with matched controls (human).

Rhesus monkeys with complete excitotoxic amygdala lesions learned object reversals as quickly as controls, contrary to earlier results with less selective lesions, but were impaired at choosing objects after the associated food was devalued, so the amygdala is critical for guiding choices after changes in reward value but not in reward contingency (monkey).

Among 489 single neurons recorded in the amygdalae of 41 neurosurgical patients, the right amygdala showed a categorical selectivity for pictures of animals that appeared independent of emotional valence or arousal (human).

Meta-analysis of fMRI and PET studies: patients with PTSD, social anxiety disorder or specific phobia consistently showed greater activity than comparison subjects in the amygdala and insula, as did healthy subjects during fear conditioning, whereas only patients with PTSD showed hypoactivation in the dorsal and rostral anterior cingulate cortices and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (human).
Veterans with PTSD showed exaggerated amygdala responses to masked fearful versus masked happy faces compared with combat-exposed veterans without PTSD (human).

In MRI of boys aged 7.5 to 18.5 years, children with autism (7.5 to 12.5 years) had larger amygdalae than typically developing children but adolescents did not differ, because the amygdala of children with autism lacked the typical age-related increase in volume; children with autism also had a larger right hippocampus (human).

In 15 healthy men, intranasal oxytocin, compared with placebo in a double-blind crossover design, potently reduced amygdala activation by fear-inducing visual stimuli and reduced coupling of the amygdala to brainstem regions implicated in autonomic and behavioral manifestations of fear (human).

In the medial amygdala, a GABAergic subpopulation promoted aggression and two other social behaviors and inhibited self-grooming, whereas neighboring glutamatergic neurons promoted repetitive self-grooming and inhibited social interactions, so inhibitory and excitatory subpopulations control social and repetitive asocial behaviors antagonistically (mouse).

Review: the amygdala has long been associated with emotion and motivation and processes both fearful and rewarding stimuli; mapping its complex anatomical connections onto behavior with causal circuit tools requires the study of its distinct circuits.

Review: work on fear conditioning pinpoints the amygdala as an important component of the system for the acquisition, storage and expression of fear memory, has elucidated how stimuli enter, travel through and exit it, and shows that findings from experimental animals apply to the human brain.

In macaque and spider monkey striate cortex, most cells were simple, complex or hypercomplex, as in the cat but with smaller receptive fields and greater sensitivity to orientation, and a few were colour coded; cells were grouped in two independent column systems, one for receptive-field orientation and one for eye preference (ocular dominance), and the simple, monocularly driven cells lay in and near layer IV (monkey).

Simultaneous recordings showed that lateral geniculate neurons connected monosynaptically to a simple cell with high probability when their receptive field lay over an elongated simple-cell subregion of the same (on or off) signature, and almost never otherwise, implying that the simple receptive field, and so orientation selectivity, is laid down at the first thalamocortical synapse (cat).

Cooling the visual cortex, which largely inactivated the cortical network but left geniculate synaptic input working, left the orientation tuning of visually evoked synaptic potentials in simple cells almost unaffected, in agreement with Hubel and Wiesel's proposal that orientation tuning arises from the arrangement of geniculate inputs (cat).

Two-photon calcium imaging at single-cell resolution showed that the centres of orientation pinwheels in visual cortex are highly ordered: neurons selective for different orientations are clearly segregated even at the very centre (cat).

Review: in monkeys, cells in visual areas 1 and 2 and in higher visual areas are segregated into three interdigitating subdivisions that differ in selectivity for colour, stereopsis, movement and orientation; the form and colour pathways derive mainly from the parvocellular and the depth and movement pathways from the magnocellular geniculate subdivisions, and human perceptual experiments are consistent with this division.

Review: a database of reported connections identifies 25 predominantly visual neocortical areas and 7 visual-association areas in the macaque, linked by 305 mostly reciprocal pathways; laminar connection patterns place them in a hierarchy of 10 cortical levels with multiple intertwined processing streams (monkey).

In PET of healthy young men, face matching and dot-location matching both activated lateral occipital cortex, whereas face matching alone activated an occipitotemporal region and location matching alone a lateral superior parietal region, evidence for separate ventral and dorsal extrastriate pathways for object recognition and spatial localization (human).

Review: proposes that the ventral stream of projections from striate to inferotemporal cortex plays the major role in the perceptual identification of objects, whereas the dorsal stream from striate to posterior parietal cortex mediates the sensorimotor transformations for visually guided actions directed at them.

A patient with a profound disorder in perceiving the shape, orientation and size of objects guided her hand and fingers strikingly accurately to the very objects whose qualities she failed to perceive, suggesting that the visual perception of object qualities and their use in controlling manual skills have distinct neural substrates (human).

Ibotenic acid lesions of the middle temporal area (MT) in rhesus monkeys caused striking elevations in thresholds for discriminating motion direction but little or no change in contrast thresholds, so activity in MT contributes selectively to motion perception (monkey).

In rhesus monkeys discriminating weak motion signals, the sensitivity of most MT neurons was very similar to the animal's psychophysical sensitivity, and single neurons typically accounted for both the absolute threshold and the shape of the psychometric function (monkey).

A patient with bilateral posterior brain damage showed a disturbance of movement vision in a rather pure form, with movement perception through hearing and touch intact; the authors attribute it to bilateral lesions of the lateral temporo-occipital cortex and underlying white matter, beyond primary visual cortex (human).

PET in normal subjects localized colour to area V4 in the lingual and fusiform gyri and visual motion to area V5 at the temporo-parieto-occipital junction, while V1 and V2 were active in all conditions, direct evidence that, as in the macaque, different prestriate areas are specialized for different attributes of vision (human).

fMRI found a region of the fusiform gyrus, in 12 of 15 subjects, that was more active for faces than for common objects and, in further tests, for intact than scrambled faces, faces than houses and faces than hands; the results rule out accounts based on attention, subordinate-level classification or animate forms, so the region is selectively involved in face perception (human).

Recording in the largest fMRI-identified face-selective region of two macaques, almost all (97%) visually responsive neurons were strongly face selective, indicating that a cortical area dedicated to face processing exists (monkey).

In macaque inferior temporal cortex, many neurons responded to virtually every stimulus, others were selective for shape, colour or texture over large receptive fields, and a separate population responded selectively to faces, depending on the configuration of facial features and tolerant of changes in size and position, most often deep in the superior temporal sulcus (monkey).

When monkeys attended to one of two stimuli inside the receptive field of a neuron in area V4 or inferior temporal cortex, the response to the unattended stimulus was dramatically reduced, whereas cells in striate cortex were unaffected by attention (monkey).

Brief microstimulation of frontal eye field sites, with currents below those that evoke saccades, enhanced the visual responses of V4 neurons whose receptive fields corresponded to the stimulated site, depending on the receptive-field stimulus and on competing stimuli, whereas stimulating non-corresponding sites could suppress V4 responses (monkey).
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): reports visual capacity in the hemianopic field after a restricted occipital ablation (human).

Phase-encoded retinotopic fMRI with cortical surface reconstruction precisely delineated the borders of human visual areas V1, V2, VP, V3 and V4 from the visual field sign, and showed that human visual areas give more weight to the centre of gaze than their monkey counterparts (human).

Review: much of human visual cortex is organized into visual field maps, identified with fMRI in medial occipital (V1, V2, V3), lateral occipital (LO-1, LO-2, hMT+), ventral occipital (hV4, VO-1, VO-2), dorsal occipital (V3A, V3B) and posterior parietal cortex (IPS-0 to IPS-4), and arranged in clusters.

In Braille readers blinded early in life, tactile discrimination tasks activated primary and secondary visual cortex, whereas sighted controls showed deactivation, and a simple tactile stimulus without discrimination activated visual areas in neither group (human).

In people blind from an early age, transient magnetic stimulation of occipital (visual) cortex induced errors in identifying Braille and embossed Roman letters and distorted tactile perceptions, whereas occipital stimulation did not affect tactile performance in sighted subjects (human).

In macaques made amblyopic by experimental strabismus or anisometropia early in life, cortical binocularity was reduced in all, and in the more severe amblyopes, visual cortex neurons driven by the amblyopic eye had substantially lower optimal spatial frequency and spatial resolution; these neuronal abnormalities alone did not explain the full range of visual deficits (monkey).

High-field fMRI during migraine visual aura in three subjects showed BOLD changes with at least eight characteristics of cortical spreading depression, starting in extrastriate area V3A and progressing slowly (about 3.5 mm/min) over occipital cortex in register with the retinotopy of the percept, strongly suggesting that an event such as spreading depression generates the aura (human).

Five patients had a progressive dementia heralded by disorders of higher visual function, eventually with alexia, agraphia, visual agnosia and components of Balint's and Gerstmann's syndromes, while memory, insight and judgement were relatively preserved until late; imaging showed predominant parieto-occipital atrophy in two, and the underlying pathology was unknown (human).

Fusiform and occipital cortex responded more to fearful than to neutral faces in healthy controls and in patients with hippocampal sclerosis, but not in patients with amygdala damage, although their visual areas were structurally intact, and the emotional response of the fusiform cortex was parametrically related to the extent of amygdala damage (human).

In mouse primary visual cortex, 4 days of monocular lid suture at postnatal day 28 caused a maximal loss of responses to the deprived eye, and these ocular dominance shifts occurred during a critical period between P19 and P32; binocular deprivation did not reduce responses, and plasticity involved both geniculocortical and intracortical connections, showing a competitive, correlation-based plasticity in the developing mouse visual cortex (mouse).

Disrupting one isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase prevented the loss of responsiveness to a briefly deprived eye in developing mouse visual cortex without affecting synaptic plasticity in vitro, and enhancing fast intracortical inhibition with benzodiazepines restored the plasticity in vivo (mouse).

In GAD65-knockout mice of all ages, and in wild-type mice before their critical period, benzodiazepines unmasked plasticity to monocular deprivation, and enhancing GABA transmission early in life made knockout mice insensitive to monocular deprivation as adults, so a threshold level of inhibition may trigger the critical period, once in life (mouse).

Chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans became organized into perineuronal nets as the critical period ended, which dark rearing delayed, and after degrading them with chondroitinase-ABC in adult rats, monocular deprivation shifted ocular dominance toward the nondeprived eye, so the mature extracellular matrix inhibits experience-dependent plasticity (rat).

Recordings in anesthetized mice showed that V1 neurons, although their receptive fields are up to one or two orders of magnitude larger than in other species, are nearly as selective for orientation and spatial frequency, include simple and complex cells, and that putative inhibitory neurons are generally less selective (mouse).

In awake head-fixed mice, most V1 neurons more than doubled their visually evoked firing when the animal ran rather than stood still, without changes in spontaneous firing or stimulus selectivity, whereas responses in the lateral geniculate nucleus did not increase with locomotion (mouse).

Locomotion activated VIP-positive neurons in mouse V1 independently of visual stimulation, largely through nicotinic input from the basal forebrain; activating VIP neurons increased V1 visual responses in stationary mice, and damaging them abolished the enhancement of V1 responses by locomotion (mouse).

In mice running in a virtual environment, layer 2/3 neurons of primary visual cortex were strongly driven by locomotion and by mismatch between actual and expected visual flow, suggesting that visual cortex may use predictive coding to detect mismatches between predicted and actual visual feedback (mouse).

Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of mouse visual cortex, characterized in vivo and then tested for connections in vitro, connected at twice the rate when they shared an orientation preference than when their preferences were orthogonal, and at much higher rates when their responses to natural stimuli were similar, pointing to fine-scale subnetworks (mouse).

Pathway tracing with receptive-field mapping showed that mouse V1 projects to 15 cortical fields, at least nine of which hold complete maps of the visual hemifield and are distinct areas; of the areas on its lateral border only LM shares the vertical meridian with V1, suggesting that LM is homologous to V2 (mouse).

Review: anatomical and physiological studies have revealed a complex network of specialized higher-order areas in mouse visual cortex, a model for studying how information is transformed across distinct processing stages.

Unlike pyramidal cells, somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons in the superficial layers of mouse visual cortex responded more when the receptive-field surround was stimulated, because horizontal cortical axons preferentially excite them, and perturbing them showed that they contribute to the surround suppression of pyramidal cells (mouse).

Optogenetically activating PV+ interneurons in mouse V1 sharpened the orientation tuning and enhanced the direction selectivity of nearby neurons and improved the animals' orientation discrimination, whereas activating somatostatin or VIP interneurons had no significant effect on selectivity (mouse).

Anterograde tracing in rhesus monkeys found pontine projections from prelunate cortex (including areas V3, PO, DP and dorsal V4d) and the posterior parahippocampal gyrus, but none from ventral V4, area TEO or the inferior temporal gyrus, so corticopontine input to the cerebellum appears to come from extrastriate areas concerned mainly with visual spatial parameters, visual motion and the peripheral visual field rather than object identification and central vision (monkey).

After large HRP injections into the macaque pontine nuclei, labelled corticopontine cells, all layer V pyramidal cells, were densest in areas 4 and 6, whereas primary visual cortex (area 17) held only a few, restricted to the region representing the lower periphery of the visual field (monkey).

In mice traversing a virtual environment, nearly half of V1 neurons were driven by a weighted sum of visual speed and run speed, and the population predicted a combination of the two better than either alone, so mouse V1 takes part in integrating visual motion and locomotion during navigation (mouse).

In seven retinotopically identified mouse visual areas, layer 2/3 populations each encoded a distinct combination of spatial and temporal frequency, orientation and direction preferences, suggesting that separate groups of areas are specialized for motion-related and pattern-related computations, perhaps analogous to dorsal and ventral streams (mouse).

Review: koniocellular neurons form a third channel in the primate lateral geniculate nucleus; in macaques the middle pair of koniocellular layers relays short-wavelength cone input to the cytochrome-oxidase blobs of V1 and the dorsal pair relays low-acuity information to layer I of V1, and koniocellular neurons that innervate extrastriate cortex are likely to sustain some visual behaviours in the absence of V1.
